INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Comm ittee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One 
Hundred Sixty-ninth Report on the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on the 
recommendations contained in the One Hundred Fifty-sixth Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2006-07) 
of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. 
2.  The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research on the recommendations contained in the One Hundred Fifty-sixth Report of the Department-related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technolo gy, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants 
(2006-07) of the Department of Scien tific and Industrial Research which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th 
May, 2006. 
3. There were twelve recommendations contained in the One Hundred Fifty-sixth Report of the Committee. Action 
Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on  
8th August, 2006 and 13th September, 2006. 
4. In the meeting held on 12th December, 2006, th e Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report and 
adopted the same. 
 
 
 
P. G. NARAYANAN 
N
EW DELHI ; Chairman, 
December 12, 2006 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

REPORT 
 The report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research 
on the recommendations contained in the One hundred and Fifty-sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the 
Department of Scientific & Industrial Research, which was presented to Parliament on 18th May, 2006. There were 12 
recommendations contained in the Report. 
 Action Taken Note on the recommendations of the Committ ee and further clarifications thereon were received 
from the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research on 8th August, 2006 and 13th September, 2006, respectively. 
 The Committee’s recommendations, Action Taken thereon by the Department and comments of the Committee 
thereon are set out in the succeeding paragraphs. 
BUDGETARY  ALLOCATION 
Recommendation 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department  has made efforts to keep the pace of expenditure 
uniform except for the first quarter for which funds were partially released. The Committee has also been assured that 
the funds for last quarter will be fully utilized. The Committee in its previous report had recommended that the 
Department evolve a mechanism to maintain uniform pace of expenditure, to the extent po ssible, throughout the year. 
The Committee hopes this healthy trend will continue in future.  
(Para 10) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 As desired by the Committee, Department would make all efforts to keep the pace of expenditure uniform during 
2006-07 also. 
 During the first quarter, the expenditure would be slightly on lower side, as the new projects are sanctioned only 
after intensive evaluation of each proposal. The expenditure in  respect of ongoing projects is based on submission of 
utilization certificates and evaluation of progress of each pr oject. After the end of the financial year, the institutions 
take time to complete the auditing. Only after auditing, they can submit the utilization certificates. 
 The funds allocated for DSIR have been utilized during the last quarter of 2005-06. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and expects the Depart ment to ensure that allotted funds are utilised 
optimally. 
IT INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT  
Recommendation 
 The Committee would like to emphasize the importance of indigenous technologies and the crucial role they are 
going to play in an increasingly globalized world. Cutting edge technologies and patentable innovations are the only 
hope for wealth generation in a cut-throat competitive envir onment. Scientific establishments of the country like the 
CSIR have a huge responsibility of training human resource to that effect and creating an enabling environment for 
such innovations to take place. The Committee is hopeful that the Council will leave no stone unturned to show 
concrete results, which can help create wealth and contribute in improving people’s life. (Para 25) 
Action Taken by the Department 

 Department appreciates the faith reposed on it by the Hon’ble Committee. At this stage CSIR is in the midst of 
formulating its Eleventh Plan and would dovetail the proposals wherever feasible for enhancing the innovation 
environment. 
Comments 
 The Committee is hopeful that CSIR in the Eleventh Plan will take due  consideration of the Committee’s 
concerns. The Committee has time and again emphasized the importance of qualitative improvements in human 
resource supply, as in a scenario where  knowledge frontiers are expanding at an exponential speed, no scientific 
establishment can afford to remain complacent. 
NATIONAL  LABORATORIES 
Recommendation 
 The Scientific research in various fields is mainly dependent on the availability of modern environment and 
major research facilities. With the global competitiveness in different fields there is a need to focus on the issues 
relating to modernization of our national laboratories. The Committee in its 142nd Report had recommended building 
of new infrastructure and renovation of the existing ones should be taken up in right earnest. The Committee would like 
to reiterate the same and would like to see renovation carried out as early as possible. The Committee recommends that 
the Council should draw a time-frame for such programme and s hould finish the task within the prescribed time-limit. 
Since the CSIR laboratories are located all over the countr y, having people’s interface in a much better way, the 
Committee recommends that there is need for setting up a special Technology Dissemination Cell in all the CSIR 
laboratories so that the technology support can be given to Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) also. (Para 31) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The concern of the Committee is taken note of. In the Tenth Plan, separate schemes on Infrastructure Renovation 
& Refurbishing (Civil) and IT Infrastructures are being implemented in a time bound manner. 
 With reference to the query on Technology Dissemination Cell in all the CSIR laboratories, it is important that a 
Unit for Science Dissemination coordinates such activities. Moreover, all the laboratories have a business development 
cell to provide technology support and transfer. 
 The Department further clarified that the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) has recommended the project 
“Building a Science knowledge Grid & ICT Infrastructure and services” on 24.10.06 and the financial sanction was 
approved by Department of expenditure on 27.01.2006 at a cost of Rs. 97.50 crore. 
 Major deliverables of the project include network enable d Desktop computers to Scientist/ staff of CSIR Labs for 
seamless integration with E-Grid / Data Centre; to facil itate the implementation of operation of e-management 
packages like e-procurement, e-finance, e-administration etc.; to facilitate Data Centre equipment & facilities for Grid 
computing infrastructure and linkage to CSIR Labs.; to faci litate the State of the art Video Conferencing Facility for 
CSIR Labs and related Scientific departments. 
 Achievements till date includes budget allocation to pr ocure Hardware such as PCs, Servers & LAN for creation/ 
modernization of ICT infrastructure, VC facility and ERP applications; preparation of common tender; specifications 
for Data Centre equipments. 
 Infrastructure Renovation & Refurbishing (Civil):  Most of the CSIR laboratories are more the 25 years old. 
For good quality research to be carried out, it is necessary to have conformance and compliance of Good Laboratory 
Practices and of various parameter standards set up by ag encies like NABL, ISO etc. These buildings should also 
adhere to the fire an d safety standards. In order to meet these requirements, a scheme namely ‘Infrastructure 
Renovation& Refurbishing (Civil)’ was put in place with an aim to upgrade the infrastructural facilities of CSIR 

laboratories. Since the approval of the scheme was received only in 2005-06. Selective renovation could only 
commence in 2006-07. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply. It also  takes note that Unit for Scie nce Dissemination coordinates the 
activities to help technology dissemination . The Committee is still of th e opinion that though all the laboratories 
have a business development cel l to provide technology support and tran sfer, there is a need for a nodal agency 
to keep track of development taking place in different laboratories for better coordination and dissemination. 
RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that there is a need to improve quality  of science education in th e country. The start has to 
be made right at the school level. Quality of science education should not only generate keen interest in children but 
also be able to fire their imagination in order to make them stick to the science stream. A holistic ‘start- to-finish’ 
approach is the need of the hour, where children once initia ted in science are not left confused after their schools but 
are provided a link to higher research institute via universities. Improving quality of research courses in Universities 
and their affiliation with research institutes, can be followed according to our own requirements. The Committee is of 
the opinion that an ambitious programme, which caters to both  the supply of rich human resource right from the school 
level and the consequential rich dividends gained by way of intellectual property finally is what should be aimed at.  
  (Para 33) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department is running a programme “CSIR Programme on Youth for Leader ship in Science (CPYLS)” to 
attract meritorious school students towards science and help them in building scientific temper and expose the young 
minds to exciting world of science. Under the programme, the first 50 students (toppe rs) from each Secondary Board 
are chosen after passing the X examination and brought to CSIR laboratories for two days for the exposure of its 
activities. Among the students who pursue science after cla ss X are being provided support and facilities to do their 
project work for class XI/XII at one of the CSIR laboratories. They are free to discuss the selection and progress of 
their project with the scientists of the laboratories and also have the access to the R&D facilities available. Amongst 
these students who secure over 90% marks in natural science subjects (physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics) in 
the Senior Secondary Examination and continue to pursue  science studies, are supported for another three years till 
graduation. They are designated as “CSIR Student Associates ” and given the facility to work on a project, in a CSIR 
laboratory of their interest during thei r vacations. Further, the Department has taken an integrated approach for the 
national human resource development for S&T by encourag ing and promoting research in the universities and 
institutions of higher learning. 
 Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) had set up a Task Force for basic scientific research in 
universities during March 2005. The Task Force had recommended inter alia: To create 10 networking centres in basic 
sciences (Physical Sciences, Chemical Sciences, Life Scie nces, Material Sciences and Mathematical Sciences) in 
leading departments of universities in different parts of th e country to provide collaborative research etc.; formal 
linkages between the universities and national level institutions including CSIR laboratories. The recommendations of 
the Task Force were accepted by MHRD and directed UGC to implement the recommendations of the Task Force for 
which an Empowered Committee has been constituted. The Empowered Committee is seized with the mechanisms of 
implementation of the recommendations of the Task Force. 
 
 

Comments 
 The Committee is hopeful that the recommendations of the task force will be taken up in the right earnest 
and the Empowered Committee appointed by the UGC will come out with an effective blue print to kick start an 
integrated programme to network high -end research that makes use of all th e available resea rch inputs in the 
country and provides necessary exposure to budding scientists. 
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY & TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT 
Recommendation 
 In a world where a substantial share of wealth produ ced is intellectual and a major portion of economy is 
knowledge-based, definition of wealth and property ha s undergone a sea change. India, being a fast-growing 
knowledge economy with a huge human resource potential, is well poised to be a leader in such a scenario. Property is 
no longer just natural and physical but increasingly intellectual. To exploit the huge intellectual capital we will have to 
ensure certain fundamentals lik e awareness and an understanding of market mechanism so that we do not lose out to 
other competitors in an envi ronment of patents and copyrights. The Comm ittee appreciates the good work done by the 
Department and hopes more results will follow in the future. (Para 41) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 In order to operate in a competitive environment, CSIR is trying to enhance awareness on some of the critical 
aspects of IP Management, namely, IP valuation, infringement detection, freedom to operate analysis, licensing, 
valorization and portfolio development. These objectives are planned to be achieved through the organization of 
workshops, conferences and training programmes for the scientists. 
Comments 
 The Committee is hopeful that the steps taken by the Department will help save our intellectual rights and 
will also ensure that products of both  modern research and traditional knowledge are not lost as a result of lack 
of awareness or knowledge of the patenting process. Th e Committee feels that the commercial interests of our 
research, including traditional knowledge, need to be protected at all costs. 
NEW MILLENIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP INITIATIVE (NMITLI) 
Recommendation 
 Progress of human civilization is based on innovation of one kind or the other. Material civilization progresses 
only with the progress in technology. Innovations require ‘out-of-the box thinking’, flexibility and an enabling 
environment. The Committee feels the above programme is a step in  the right direction. It is of the opinion that there is 
a need to take care of grass root innovations as small beginni ngs have big results. Beside this, in an era of intellectual 
property, innovations and weal th are necessarily linked and,  therefore, the stress on innovation cannot be over 
emphasized. (Para 44) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department appreciates the Standing Committee’s comments on innovation particularly the grass root 
innovations to generate wealth. The National Innovation Foundation (NIF), Ahmedabad, a registered society, is 
engaged in scouting, documenting, augmenting and adding value to the innovations and traditional knowledge of the 
innovations at the grass root level. NIF is also preparin g a national register of outstanding traditional knowledge and 
contemporary green grass root innovations. 
 CSIR and NIF have entered into an MoU to institute the “CSIR-NIF Innovation Fellowship” to provide hand 
holding support to grass root innovators and traditional knowledge holders. The selected innovations are being taken up 

by CSIR laboratories for value addition with a view to transform such innovations and knowledge into employment and 
wealth generating opportunities. 
Comments 
 The Committee feels that the country requires more and more institutional support systems like the 
National Innovation Foundation (NIF), Ahmedabad, to support grass root scientific breakthroughs so that such 
groundbreaking discoveries are not lost on account of lack of support. What is also required is awareness about 
the availability of such support so th at maximum use of such infrastructure is made for generating wealth for 
individual innovators in particular and society in general. 
INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that a developing country like India ne eds basic infrastructure to serve the needs of a fast 
growing economy which needs even further impetus to meet the needs of teeming millions. Development, being an 
integrated process, has a multiplier effect on the economy and growth. Improvement in our scientific infrastructure is of 
utmost importance, as good research requires good laboratories and other logistic support. (Para 47) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Expenditure and Finance Comm ittee (EFC) has approved the project  “Building a Science knowledge Grid & 
ICT infrastructure and services” in January 2006. The project aims to provide network enabled Desktop computers to 
Scientist / staff of CSIR Laboratories for seamless inte gration with E-Grid / Data Centre; to facilitate the 
implementation of operation of e-mana gement packages like e-procurement, e-finance, e-administration etc.; to 
facilitate Data Centre equipment and facilities for Grid computing and linkage to CSIR Labs.; to facilitate the State-of-
the-art Video Conferencing facility for CSIR Laboratories and related departments. 
 It is expected after the successful completion of the project the information flow and decision support system in 
the organization would be well equipped. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the view that the Knowledge Grid should be comple ted as soon as possible so that 
information roadblocks could be removed and scientific research be facilitated. 
TECHNOLOGY PROMOTION, DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION (TPDU) PROGRAMMES 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that the Department should make efforts to encourage more participation from the Industry 
with a good track record for distribution of both risks and rewards. Industry with a rich experience of market can help 
scientific establishments feel the pulse of the market and make scientific research commercially viable. (Para 55) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Technology Development and Demonstration Progra mme (TDDP) of DSIR is specifically intended to 
encourage participation of industry in developing products/ processes and absorption of imported technologies. The 
Scheme supports lab scale/ bench scale technologies developed by CSIR, National Laboratories/ Institutions and 
Universities for scale up and commercialization by Indian industries. 
 The projects are submitted, for partial financial support, by the industry on its own or in association with national 
laboratories like IITs, IISc. and Universities. The scheme has been instrumental in establishing linkages amongst 
national laboratories, scientific institutions and industries and making scientific research commercially viable. 

 As suggested by the Committee, the Department would make further efforts by giving wide publicity to the 
programme for enhancing the interaction with Scientific establishments and industrial units to formulate joint 
technology development and demonstration projects to benefit from each other’s expertise. 
 With this in view, the Department periodically inserts advertisements in national dailies (a) covering all 
departmental schemes and also (b) covering individual schemes. 
 Last year 12 TV programmes were developed and broadcasted through Doordarshan. 
 Apart from 2-days national conference on research and de velopment in industries organized every year in Delhi, 
eleven one-day seminars with exhibition on innovations were held in smaller towns with industry clusters. These events 
always had a large draw. About ten such events will be held in 2006-07. 
 DSIR has been arranging exhibition spaces in associ ation with ITPO in the IITF every year for industries. 
Besides, in association with CII, facilities were provided to Indian industries to exhibit their technologies abroad. This 
year, DSIR facilitated participation of Indian industries in the Hannover Fair also. 
Comments 
 The Committee appreciates the effort made by the Department to comme rcialize infant technologies and 
involve industry in such an endeavour.  The Committee is of the view that ultimate test of a newly developed 
technology is it’s commercial viability. 
DEVELOPING NEW GENERATION FUELS 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is of the view that the research on altern ative sources of energy is still at infant stage. Where 
success has been achieved, commercial feasibility is a big problem. Given the volatile situation of fossil fuels, spiraling 
prices of crude oil; environmental concerns and expensive nature of nuclear fuel sooner or later the country will have to 
turn to non-conventional energy sources for its future needs.  The efforts made in this direction may be a good start but 
there is a long way to go. A non-conven tional source of energy, wh ich is commercially viab le, environment-friendly 
and capable of changing the present pattern of fuel consumption, is the only solution in the long run. (Para 59) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department has initiated a network programme on Development of new generation fuels and lubricants 
during Tenth Five Year Plan. CSIR through its various laboratories has been working on biofuels (ethanol) and 
biodiesel. The technologies are at various stages of developments. Biodiesel developed by the Department conforms to 
Euro emission norms. 
 The Department further clarified that CSIR has initiated a programme in the Tenth FYP for developing liquid 
fuels and ethanol produced from biomass. This is one of the major activities of the network project ‘Developing new 
generation fuels and lubricants’ approved with a total co st of Rs.24.05 crores. The programme envisages use of 
agriculture wastes such as wheat straw, rice straw, bagasse  etc. instead of molasses whose availability in India is 
predicted to be insufficient. CSIR is also working on performance evaluation of new generation automotive fuels to 
meet the emission norms. 
Achievements so far: 
 Ethanol produced from rice, wheat flour using commercial thermostable enzyme and yeast at 10L scale. 
 Isolation and identification of thermophilic strains that grow at 50°C. 
 Produce ethanol from starch by simultaneous liquification, saccaharification and fermentation by using 
thermophiles. 

 Analysis of fermented hydrolysate containing poly-, tr i-, di- and monosaccharides with ethanol in single 
HPLC run. 
 14 fold increase in cellulase production by SSF process using T. reesei was achieved. 140 FPUs of cellulase 
produced per gm of wheat bran compared to global average of 200 FPUs /g pure cellulose or lactose. 
 Novel substrate (Water Hyacinth) used in cellulase production. 
 New Strain with improved BGL activity isolated. 
 Strategy for genetic improvement of T reesei formulated and works initiated. 
 Sugar fatty acid ester, sugar amine, cellulose ester and starch esters prepared as lube base stock. 
Bio fuels 
 Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP), a constituent of CSIR has carried out field studies with ethanol-gasoline 
blends with IOC R&D, Faridabad. These studies on ethanol we re carried out in earlier (1980s) technology vehicles and 
fuels. 
 In early nineties, Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy  Sources (MNES) sponsored a study on use of ethanol in 
diesel bus fleet of DTC running on dual-fuel mode using IIP developed retrofit kit for induction of ethanol. The results 
of this study showed feasibility of replacing 14.9% of diesel by ethanol and smoke reduction of up to 40%. 
Biodiesel 
 CSIR has been investing on development of ‘Biodiesel’ for quite some time and have established competencies 
in many areas of its production and use. These include en d-to-end use i.e., growing of bioresource as well as its 
extraction and conversion into diesel as fuel. The detail of the work carried out by CSIR is given below: 
    a.  Generation of Plantation material: 
 Inadequate seed availability is a major problem. Jatropha Curcus was never grown in organized sector and there 
is very little information available on germplasm, if at all, besides the problem of composition and consistency. One 
germplasm, which grows in one part of India, may not fruit in other region. Also, there are wide variations in seed yield 
and oil content. 
 NBRI, Lucknow has made a concerted effort in collecti ng germplasm from various states, creating nursery trails 
of germplasm, nursery experiments and raising successful nurse ries of selected materials. It has raised 3 lakh plants 
from its selections. 
 RRL, Jorhat in the hilly terrain of North-East and CSMCRI, in the waste lands of Gujarat and Orissa have also 
made efforts in identifying elite varieties of Jatropha Curcus in these regions. 
    b.  Extraction of oil 
 This is an important area wherein the oil purity and yi eld will have an impact on the cost of biodiesel and the 
byproduct. NBRI, has developed protocols for extraction of oil from Jatropha. 
    c. Storage and transportation 
 No authentic data is available on shel f life of Jatropha seeds, oil and biodiesel in India. NBRI has been engaged 
in generating data on storage of oil under various conditions. IICT has expertise and experience in similar activities, 
which can be used to generate data on shelf life of seeds, oils and biodiesel. 
    d.  Biodiesel production/ transesterification/ blending 
 CSIR laboratories have been doing R&D on transeterification and have successfully converted jatropha oil to 
biodiesel matching international specifications. IIP, Dehradun has developed three batch processes for low Free Fatty 

Acid (FFA) as well as for high FFA contents. Efforts are on to develop continuous transeterificiation process. IICT is 
doing R&D on catalyst free process as well as on solid catalys t. CSMCRI has designed plan ts for rural cooperatives. 
Blending of biodiesel with diesel is another area where expertise exists in IICT and IIP. 
    e.  Testing of blends 
 IIP, Dehradun and CSMCRI have already initiated testing blends of Diesel/Biodiesel for emissions and engine 
performance. While IIP is testing blends on engine performance vis-a-vis emissions, CSMCRI, has studied the engine 
performance of vehicle run over 6000 km. 
    f.  Effective generation / utilization of by products 
 Value addition to the Jatropha oil cake, which is a no n-edible matter, is another important area. CSMCRI in 
collaboration with Anand Agriculture University, has establis hed that cake has dual role of manure-cumbiopesticide. 
Besides developing cake as fertilizer, NBRI is collaborating wi th industry to make it a substitute for coal. Glycerine, 
which is a byproduct of transesterification needs to be of high purity. liP and CSMCRI are working on this aspect in the 
transesterification technology development. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Depa rtment will continue to make vigorous efforts in 
this direction. 
SETTING UP A WORLD CLASS DRUG RESEARCH INSTITUTE 
Recommendation 
 A country still not free from diseases which acquire epidemic proportions, a research programme for drug 
development cannot be overemphasized. Given the fact that major chunk of people suffering from such diseases are the 
ones with least purchasing power makes the challenge doubly complex. Government funded research institutes, not 
being solely driven by profit motive, are not left with a choice but to shoulder the responsibility, along with other 
departments of the Government, of providing affordable drugs  as no multi-national company will venture into an area 
where rich returns are not possible. The Committee is of the vi ew that what is required is  a close coordination between 
different arms of the Government as individual departments cannot be expected to bring down the cost of drugs below 
a level. The Committee feels that innovative ways like distribu tion of cost by providing cheap insurance for diseases to 
people have to be devised, as cost of manufacturing of drugs cannot be brought down below a point. (Para 61) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The suggestions of the Committee are under consideration of  Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers which is the 
administrative ministry for this issue. It is hoped that new Pharmaceutical and Drugs Policy will address this issue 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Department would pursue the Committee’s suggestion 
with the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers, and also keep the Committee apprised of such follow up. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is also of the opinion that the traditional medicine is popular, accepted and used by most of the 
country’s population. Moreover, there is growing importance in  traditional health systems in providing health care for 
wider population. Inspite of the Department’s efforts in formulating Golden Triangle, there is a need for giving boost to 
the herbal medicines. The Committee feels that with the abu ndant resources of medicinal plants all over the country 
there is a need to set up a Herbal Research and Developm ent Institute in a location where all the variation of our 
biodiversity can be tapped. (Para 62) 

Action Taken by the Department 
 There are over 7 lakhs registered Prac titioners of Ayurveda System in the country who are providing Health Care 
facilities in the country. On an average, for 1600 po pulation there is one A YUSH doctor. Department of AYUSH is 
committed to promote and propagate Ay urveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani,  Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) 
system of medicines in India and abroad. Some of our products like Isabgol, Senna etc. and Panchkarma therapy are 
doing very well at International level also. Department is following strategy of providing seats for foreign national in 
educational institutions, taking up the matter at Gove rnment level regarding recognition of AYUSH system of 
medicine, sending experts to teach Ayur veda in foreign countries etc. The De partment of AYUSH is supporting NGOs 
to promote strength of AYUSH system by organizing, workshops. Health Melas are being organized to create 
awareness among the general public about the efficacy and cost effectiveness of AYUSH DRUGS and easy availability 
of herbs and Plants. With a view to promote this system through electronic media, Department has released 51 video 
spots on different system of medicine under AYUSH for tele cast over National network and other channels on Delhi 
Doordarshan. Department of AYUSH has been successfully organizing Arogya, a comprehensive exhibition on 
AYUSH system of medicine at Delhi for th e last 5 years and is now also organizing Arogya in different states of the 
country. Arogya in Chennai was organized in January 2005 and Arogya in Hyderabad in November 2005. The 
Department of AYUSH is also exploring the possibilities of or ganizing Arogya in other cities of the country. Further to 
implementing schemes of Hospital and Dispensaries under which Financial Assistance is given to the States to open 
AYUSH clinic by Allopathic Hospitals and supply of Ayurvedic medicines to Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha and 
Homeopathic Dispensaries. 
 Under Golden Triangle Partnership of AYUSH, CSIR and ICMR, the state-of-the-art research is being 
undertaken on important diseases: 
 Ensuring the conservation, organic cultivation and availability of quality raw material at affordable price, 
Government of India has set up National Medicinal Plants Boar d in the year 2000. The Board is also responsible to co-
ordinate with Ministries /Departments/Organisations/States/UT governments for development of medicinal plants 
sector. During the last five years NMPB has sanctioned approximately 4258 projects for developing the medicinal 
plants sector in the country for which an amount of appr oximately Rs. 100 crores has already been released. Many 
projects have also been sanctioned to R&D institutions to CSIR like as RRL, Jammu; RRL, Jorhat; CIMAP, Lucknow; 
NBRI, Lucknow and IHBT, Palampur. 
 As regards setting up Herbal Research & Development inst itute, CSIR already has premier research institutes like 
CIMAP, RRL, Jammu, NBRI & CDRI which are engaged in re search in various areas relating to medicinal plants. 
However, a State-of- the-art research institution exclusively for research and development of herbal drugs devoted to 
state of the art research on Pharmacopo ial standards development of chemical /bio-logical markers/ chromatogram / 
fingerprints, drug development standardization and quality control would go a long way in scientific validation of 
traditional Medicinal systems and obtaining a fresh share of global herbal trade. This could be a collaborative enterprise 
of Department of AYUSH and CSIR. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the opinion that despite the effo rts made by the Department, not enough progress has 
been made in the area of alternativ e system of medicine. Allopathy along with its long-term side effects and 
expensive nature still remains the pref erred option on account of non-availa bility of alternative solutions in 
many disease areas and lack of standardization. We have to go a long way in developing alternative system of 
medicine for the benefit of the common man. 
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF CHEMICAL BIOLOGY, KOLKATA (IICB) 
 The Committee held discussions with the officials of Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Kolkata on 5th 
February, 2005. During the course of the discussion, the Committee was informed that the Institute has taken up 

research in the field of cancer and sign ificant progress has been achieved as a herbal molecule has been identified to 
kill chronic meylogenous lukemic cells. The Committee, was informed that: 
 “The molecule identified by IICB Scientists from Paan has shown in experimental conditions a beneficial affect 
for chronic meylogenous luikemic cells (CML), a kind of blood cancer. The institute has to do a lot more work on the 
molecule so that it can be passed to pharmaceutical sector for production.” 
Recommendation 
 In pursuance of the above statement of  the IICB and also in view of the discussion it had with the management of 
IICB, Kolkata, the Committee strongly recommends that since cancer is the most difficult disease to treat in medical 
science and different types of cancer require different types of medicines, the Institute should put optimum effort to 
develop this molecule of paan to a final drug stage as soon as possible so that it could be passed on to the 
pharmaceutical sector for production in the near future thereby transmitting a lot of benefit to medical sector in treating 
chronic cases of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML.) (Para 64) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 A total number of 21 patent applications in different countries on the crude Piper betel leaf extract and the 
purified molecule have been licensed out to Nicholas Piramal India Ltd (NPIL). NPIL is working on the two 
approaches: Development of Piper betel leaf extract and the pure molecule for the treatment of chronic myeloid 
leukemia (CML) patents. According to NPIL, the extract sh owed significant anti-tumor activity in drug-sensitive and 
drug-resistant cells obtained from CML patients. NPIL is going to conduct GLP toxicity studies and human clinical 
trials with the extract soon. The pure compound showed co mparable activity to the only drug available, Gleevee in in 
vivo assays. However, the bioavailability of the compound in oral route is poor. NPIL is working upon development of 
formulations to improve the bioavailability for developing marketable oral product. 
Comments 
 The Committee hopes that the effort by the Department will bear fruit in due course of time and will prove 
to be of immense benefit to a section of humanity suffering from chronic myeloid leukemia (CML.). The 
Committee is also optimistic abou t the oral route of the breakthr
ough though till now it has not been very 
successful.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment
 and Forests having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Seventeenth Report of
 the Committee. This Report examines the Annual Report (1993-94) of the Department of Biotechnology with Particular
 reference: to the development of immunodiagnostic kits; environmental conservation and biodiversity; medicinal and
 aromatic plants; and implications of new GATT regime and Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) with regard to new
 developments in Biotechnology.
2. The Committee held in all three meetings on January 5, 6 and March 29, 1995. In the meeting held on January 5, 1995
 Secretary, Department of Biotechnology gave a brief presentation about the activities of his Department, particularly in the
 aforementioned four areas selected by the Committee for examination. The Members also raised certain queries with regard to
 the various programmes supported by the department of Biotechnology. In the meeting held on January 6, 1995, further
 discussion took place on the Annual Repot of the Department of Biotechnology. The Secretary and the representatives of the
 Department of Biotechnology furnished answers to the questions raised by the Members on the previous day.
3. The Committee thanks the officials of the Department of Biotechnology for giving it necessary information and placing
 before the Committee relevant papers/background notes which facilitiated the Committee to undertake an in-depth
 examination of the Annual Report (1993-94) of the Department of Biotechnology and commends the Department for its
 excellent work.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its meeting held on the 29th March, 1995.

March 29, 1995
SYED SIBTEY RAZI

Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
REPORT
 
General Background
 
Biotechnology is a fast growing area of science which has great potential for major applications in the fields of
 agriculture and food, health care, industry, environment, etc. It will have an important role to play in the conservation and
 utilisation of biodiversity including the preservation and propagation of medicinal and aromatic plants. The immediate
 major impact of biotechnology in the medical field relates of the development of immunodiagnostic kits, vaccines, and
 major drugs.
 
2. The Committee was informed about the new initiatives taken by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) during the
 year 1993-94, which included programmes in the area of human gentics, transgenic research relating to both animals and
 plants, protein engineering, food biotechnology, etc.
 
3. While examining the Annual Report of the Department of Biotechnology for the year 1993-94, the Committee
 decided to focus its attention on the programmes in the areas of: development of immunodiagnostic kits; environmental
 conservation and biodiversity; and medicinal and aromtic plants. The Committee also considered the implications of new
 GATTregime and Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) with regard to new developments in biotechnology.
 
lmmunodiagnostic Kits
 
4. DBT supports R&D for producing safe, low cost, efficacious diagnostic kits, particularly for early detection of
 communicable diseases, both in human beings and animals. The Secretary, DBT gave a detailed account of the progress
 made by the Department in the development of various immunodiagnostic kits. According to him the diagnostics industry
 is making rapid progress globally and the turnover of this industry is picking up very fast. During the year 1993-94, there
 had been an impressive growth in India of over 80 per cent in monetary value over the previous year; the estimated annual
 turnover at manufacturers' prices was placed at Rs. 135 crore. The technology in this area is also moving very fast with
 the availability of diagnostics based on Deoxyribo Nucleic Acid (DNA) probes and polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
 techniques. PCR based kits have been recently introduced on an experimental basis by one of the companies. Through the
 promotional efforts of and financial support provided by DBT, the Committee learnt that kits for kala azar, malaria,
 filariasis, HIV kits, tuberculosis probes, aspergillosis and hepatitis A are under various stages of development, validation
 and commercialization. The National Institute of Immunology (NII) has developed a dot Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent
 Assay (ELISA) method for the detection of haemolytic streptococus infection in children which has been transferred to
 M/S Nicolas India Limited, Bombay. ELISA method for the detection of antigens of E. histolytica in amoebic liver
 abscess has been developed and transferred to M/S Cadilla Lab. Ltd., Ahmedabad. Similarly, kit for the detection of
 salmonella typhi in blood has been developed and transferred to M/S Lupin, Bombay. Formats for the early detection of
 pregnancy have been transferred to M/S Ranbaxy Laboratories-Ltd., Delhi. As a result of the programmes initiated by the
 Department, three kits are already in the market which include kits for early detection of pregnancy, amoebiasis and
 leishmaniasis.
4.1 Secretary, DBT informed the Committee that the Delhi component of the International Centre for Genetic
 Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB) had recently developed a highly efficient kit for the diagnosis of HIV'I and II.
 The sensitivity of this kit is 100 per cent and the specificity is 98.7 per cent. The Committee was also told the prototype
 diagnostic kits for animal and poultry diseases were also under various stages of development.
5. The Committee wanted to know whether the microplate ELISA and dot ELISA techniques for the detection of kala
 azar had been standardised to industrial scale, and if this had not been done, whether the Department had set any time-
frame for it. To this, the representative of the Department replied that in order to shift from mouse to in vitro, for large
 scale production, more research was required to be done. DBT was already seized of the problem, and it might take about
 two to three years to perfect this technique through in vitro culture. The anti-body detection kit for kala azar developed by
 the Ceraral Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow, has, however, been transferred to M/S Span Diagnostic, Surat, and
 the Company has already commenced production of this kit.
6. As regards development of HIV kit, the Committee was informed that the Department was considering developing
 the kit indigenously. DBT had invited three experts and gave them a contract for two years. The work is going on at: Nil,
 New Delhi; South Campus, University of Delhi; and the Cancer Research Institute, Bombay. The Committee was assured
 that the progress in these three projects was quite satisfactory. At Nil, prototype kits have been developed, and have been
 evaluated for 100 per cent sensitivity and 100 per cent specificity. These kits are likely to be ready by July, 1995. DBT, in
 consultation with Nil, is making efforts to commercialize them. At the South Delhi Campus of Delhi University, the
 efforts at present relate to assembling prototype kits, and it would take at least one more year to standardise the format. At

17th Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/17threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:58]
 the Cancer Research Institute, Bombay, Western Blot Kits are being developed using wholesale viral lysate of HIV I virus
 grown in lymphocytes.
7. About the DNA probes for the early detection of tuberculosis, the Committee was told that the probes developed by
 NII and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) use radioactivity. The probes of Nil have about 90 per cent
 specificity and about 87 per sensitivity. To make them available for the National TB Control Programme both Nil and
 AIIMS are doing further research, and the work at Nil is in a fairly advanced stage. There is, however, a problem with
 regard to the use of DNA probes, because these require highly trained and skilled manpower to use them. DBT is already
 in touch with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and is trying to persuade the Ministry to make use of these
 probes initially in the hospitals. In response to a pointed question regarding the availability of the non-radioactive kit, the
 representative of the Department told that it should be possible to make it available by the end of 1995.
7.1 The Committee impressed on the Department to develop the non-radioactive kit which can be easily made
 available for the National TB Control Programme. DBT may also explore the possibility of using the existing probes in
 hospital conditions where trained technical manpower is available, and for this the Department should take up the matter
 with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
8. DBT stated that efforts are being made to shift away from animal-based production to genetic engineering-based
 production, as this was an area of great opportunity and there is already a powerful lobby against the use of animals in
 scientific experiments; the representative of the Department informed the Committee that in some specific projects at Nil
 genetic approaches were being used. For example, in screening for immunomodulator, vaccine development genetic
 approaches were being used. In the coming two to three years, it would be possible to shift from animal based system to
 genetic approaches.
      8. 1 The Committee is of the view that the initiative taken by the Department to shift from animal-based production to
 genetic engineering-based production is praiseworthy. Although the genetic approach is a difficult one, the Committee
 feels that it is an area of great opportunity. If DBT can achieve success in this area, so that one can reduce animal-based
 experiments and production it would be a major achievement; such an approach would prove highly beneficial in the long
 run. The Committee would strongly support these efforts.
9. To a question whether pert charts for the development leading to production of all the immunodiagnostic kits have
 been prepared by the Departments the Committee was informed that, while sanctioning the project, the time-schedule was
 fixed. After every six months, a review of the project was also conducted.
9.1 The Committee expresses its happiness over the range of areas in which efforts are being made by the Department
 to develop immunodiagnostic kits. It emphasised that a set time frame be fixed for development of these kits. The
 Committee noted the progress made in the area of development of detection kit for kala azar, diagnostic test for detection
 of circulating antigen in human filariasis and HIV detection kits, etc; but felt strongly that the Department should be able
 to draw-up a time-schedule by which the kits supported or developed by it would be available. DBT should, therefore,
 introduce pert charts for all the immunodiagnostic kits, as this would enable it to properly monitor the progress achieved
 in this area. The Committee fully appreciates the difficulties which one fates with regard to the development of biological
 systems; however, tight monitoring has to be introduced since development of low cost, easily used immunodiagnostic
 kits for common diseases is a priority area of DBT.
10. With regard to protype diagnostic kits for animal and poultry disease, the Committee was given an account of the
 prototype formats which have been prepared, and techniques which are being transferred to the industry. Work on
 standardisation of reagents, conjugates, shelf life of the plates, etc. has been taken up.
10.1 The Committee is of the view that Indian scientists and Indian industry must try to obtain the best that is available
 out of modern biotechnological advances. It was noted that there is the Centre for Biochemicals, Delhi, which has been
 given the responsibility by DBT to start producing many recombinant agents, restriction enzymes, etc.; in addition there is
 the Bangalore based Gene, Lupin and many such industries which are now coming forward to produce these agents. In the
 view of the Committee DBT should obtain information on work done elsewhere in the world relating to biotechnology
 and the requirements for this work are not only for research but also for production in terms of chemicals and biologicals,
 of various types. It should then arrange for research in the country to develop these, or where appropriate arrange for
 transfer of technology from abroad. The efforts should be to have as much of these produced in the country since easy
 availability of these items of high quality underpin all developments in this field.
11. The Committee is firmly of the view that there is need to bring in the industry, particularly in the area of
 immunodiagnostics, at a fairly early stage, both from the viewpoints of estimating market demand and from the viewpoint
 of the technologies relating ultimately to production. By carrying out field trials, with small quantities of materials one
 can say that results have been successful at the laboratory scale, but when the industry comes into the picture, it requires
 larger quantity of input materials and the availability and costs of these become important. This can then change the whole
 scenario. The Department should, therefore, examine the entire area from the viewpoint of market demand, technology of
 production and inputs required for production. It would be dearly desirable to bring in industry on an overlapping basis
 with the research effort. The Committee noted that the Department was making good efforts in this direction; the fact that
 the Biotechnology Consortium Limited was created to bring an overlap between R&D on the one hand and production
 and trade on the other is indicative of this. The Committee would like the Department to strengthen this area further.

Medicinal and Aromatic Plants
 
12. The Committee was informed by the Secretary, DBT that India has about 1600 plant species of' medical value and
 about 250 species of aromatic value. A number of agencies like the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, Indian
 Council of Medical Research, Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, Ministries of Environment and Forests and
 Health and Family Welfare are working on different aspects of medicinal and aromatic plants. The programmes which are
 being supported by the Department focus on the generation techniques for endangered medicinal plants and in vitro
 propagation. The Department is also supporting the biotransformation for production of phytochemicals, and product
 development through gene cloning and related techniques. A detailed proposal for
 the establishment of gene bank for medicinal and aromatic plants among G-15 countries was approved at the Heads of
 Government's meeting at Caracas, Venezuela in 1991. Under the proposal India is the overall coordinator for the
 programme. Under the G-15 agreements, DBT is acting as the regional coordinator of the project for arranging meetings
 of the Scientific Advisory Committees and Regional Coordination Committees and is publishing newsletters, besides
 organising training courses for the G-15 countries.
12.1 For germ plasm conservation three National Gene Banks have been set up. These Gene Banks are located at the
 Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic, Plants (CIMAP), Lucknow; National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources
 (NBPGR), New Delhi; and Tropical Botanical Garden and Research Institute (TBGRI), Trivandrum.
13. The Committee was informed by the representative of the Department that apart from a number of government
 agencies, Companies like Hamdard, Dabur, Zandu, Himalayan Drug House are working in the area of medicinal and
 aromatic plants. The Department of Biotechnology has a Task Force, to ensure proper coordination amongst various
 agencies.                                                                                                                           
      14. Regarding the programme on immunomodulators of plants origin, the Committee wastold that the work had been
 taken up at Nil very recently and significant progress had been made in identifying a number of compounds. As many as
 five compounds have been isolated from 'amla' and 'pipli'.
      15. The Committee was informed that as part of the G-15 agreement, an inventory for medicinal plants for India had
 been prepared. It had been planned to identify initially only 27 plants on which work will start, and this cam be updated
 after three years.
      15.1 The Committee appreciated that 27 plants have been included in the inventory of medicinal plants. It, however
 feels that efforts should be made on a continuous basis to identify more such plants.
      16. The Committee feels that modalities may be finalised to enable the three gene banks established in the country to
 have appropriate exchange arrangements with other gene banks for which coordinators are Brazil and Egypt. The National
 Gene Banks may also think on the possibility of sending material to farmers and other interested parties subject to the
 existing rules and regulations in the matter.
      17. The representative of DBT informed the Committee that, a brain-storming session was/organisedby DBT on March
 5-6, 1993 to evolve a number of projects on medicinal and aromatic plants. Apart from scientists, this session was
 attended by distinguished Ayurvedic specialists as well. Besides, experts from Ayurveda and Unani Councils, other
 clinicians were also present in this session. As a result of the brain-storming session, the Department has identified the
 criteria by which plants should be taken up for further work, and which require biotechnological inputs. The areas which
 the Department has identified include those plants which have potential as also proven medicinal value. In addition, plants
 which are getting endangered and require large scale preservation and conservation, as also those plants where R&D leads
 are available and where further research is needed, have been identified.
17.1 The Committee was happy that DBT had arranged such a get together involving those from the indigenous
 systems; it desired a continuing follow up of the result of the aforesaid brain-storming session.
      17.2 The Committee also feels that DBT should look into the holistic approach that Characterises the use of the
 medicinal and aromatic plants in indigenous systems. There are many components in these plants which act together on
 the human or animal system, where also there are many components involved in defining a state of health or of disease.
 This is different from the "active principles" and "targetted approach" that defines western medical science.
      18. The committee is of the view that Ayurveda has great strength. Ayurvedic products are an important area in which
 one should be able to obtain patents. DBT should clearly spell out its priorities in this area. The Department should in
 association with other concerned national agencies arrange to combine the modern biotechnological approach with the
 traditional holistic approach. The modern approach should result in ensuring quality which is very important. The
 Department should also consider associating private enterprises in this field.
      19. Being basically "a scientific department, the difficulties faced by DBT in ascertaining the market requirements of
 products based on medicinal plants are real. This information is vital for large scale cultivation of various plants which
 then are used for producing medical products.
      19.1 Since many other government agencies and research institutions are working in the area of medicinal and
 aromatic plants, the Committee feels that DBT may think of setting up of a Central organisation which could prepare a
 demand profile of various medicinal and aromatic plant-based products.

 Environmental Conservation and Biodiversity
 
      20. The Department of Biotechnology is also working in the area or environmental conservation and biodiversity.
 ELISA/PCR techniques and DNA probes have been developed for the detection of pathogenic viruses and bacteria in
 drinking water. These kits are under field evaluation. The Committee was also told about biosurfactants
, microbial
 desulphurisation of gaseous fuels, biosensors for detection of pesticides as other important developments. The Department
 is supporting programmes for biodiversity conservation in different agro-climatic zone, extraction of nuclear DNA, tissue
 culture protocol for Jojoba, etc. The Committee was also informed that new programmes for important ecosystems such
 as Alpine flora, and flora of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands were being formulated.
      21. The representative of the Department informed the Committee that, with regard to environmental conservation and
 biodiversity, various techniques have been developed by different Institutes with the support of DBT. For example, the
 ELISA, PCR techniques and DNA probes were developed for the detection of pathogenic viruses, bacteria and E.
 histolytica which have been field tested by National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), Nagpur in
 collaboration with the state municipal authorities of Tamil Nadu and Delhi. The techniques were developed with the
 contributions of AIIMS, Jawaharlal Nehru University and Nil.
      21.1 The Committee is of the view that the new techniques and probes developed for the detection of pathogenic
 viruses, bacteria and E. histolytica can play an important role in assessing water quality. "The Committee recommends
 that these techniques should be put to actual use by encouraging their large scale use.
 
      22. The Committee is happy to note that under several DBT supported programmes in environmental biotechnology,
 NEERI, Nagpur has applied for a number of patents. For example, the process for the deemulsification of oil in water
 emulsion for the recovery of oil, industrial waste water utilisation and an improved process for desulphurisation of coal
 are important technologies developed by NEERI. The Committee recommends that proper information technology
 packages should be prepared on the technologies developed by NEERI for use by industry and efforts may be made to
 pass on these technologies to industry for their commercialisation.
 
      23. On being asked about the progress made relating to the development of biosensors for detection of pesticides in
 water using the potentiometric techniques, the Committee was informed that the biosensors have already been developed
 and are being field-tested and that it will take about two years for field evaluation and finalisation of the" technology
 package.
 
      23.1 The detection of biopesticides through biosensors is a new area. The Committee is happy to note that efforts are
 being made to obtain feedback from farmers and those in the field and, in the light of the feedback received, defects, if
 any, found in the present kit would be rectified.
 
      24. The Committee also feels that certain technologies pertaining to the environment sector which have been perfected
 at the laboratory scale can be really regarded as significant achievements only when they are made available for large
 scale production and use. Since, at laboratory level, many of the technologies have been proven, concerted efforts should
 now be made to make these technologies commercially viable.
 
      25. Biotechnology is a fast developing frontier are of science, and of technology. Accordingly the Department of
 Biotechnology will have to look in detail about the implications of the new GATT regime and land IPR aspects with
 regard to the developments that are planned for the country in the area of biotechnology. In this presentation, the
 Secretary, DBT, gave a detailed account of the implications of new GATT regime and IPR aspects with regard to new
 developments in biotechnology. He informed the Committee about the various advantages and disadvantages flowing
 from the new arrangement in the field of agriculture, particularly of seeds and in the area of human/animal health. The
 Secretary stated that the question of patenting in the biological field was different from other areas like electronics,
 computers, physical or chemical science. At present, there is only one cell in the CSIR system which has some expertise
 in the area of patents. DBT has been taking help from this Cell. It has been decided that initially all the scientific
 departments would
d support in strengthening this Cell, and later on, when adequate expertise has been developed, the
 country will have four or five centres at different places which will provide help to the scientists. He also mentioned that
 the Government had decided to strengthen the Patent Offices, and at Nagpur there will be a Patent Information Office
 where all the information on world patents would be available. In the context of patent awareness, the Secretary informed
 the Committee about a seminar organised at NII which was arranged in collaboration with the World Intellectual Property
 Rights Organisation.
      25.1 The Committee is firmly of the view that the Department of Biotechnology should arrange for a system to
 understand patent laws and their implications in so far as applicable to living organisms. Patenting in the biological area is
 very different from what is done in the other fields of science and technology. There are many grey areas when it come to

 area of IPR in biological sciences. This should relate also to identifying what part of our research can be patented
 nationallyI as also internationally, and what support this activity should receive from the Government. This group should
 examine the developments taking place internationally, and advise Government and our scientific community on the

 skills in this area, and be supported by Government for the same.

Summary of Recommendations/Observations
 
1. The Committee impressed on the Department to develop the non-radioactive kit which can be easily made available
 for the National TB Control Programme. DBT may also explore the possibility of using the existing probes in hospital
 conditions where trained technical manpower is available, and for this the Department should take up the matter with the
 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

            2. The Committee is of the view that the initiative taken by the Department to shift from animal-based production to
 genetic engineering-based production is praiseworthy. Although the genetic approach is a difficult one, the Committee feels
 that it is an area of great opportunity. If DBT can achieve success in this area, so that one can reduce animal-based
 experiments and production it would be a major achievement; such an approach would prove highly beneficial in the long
 run. The Committee would strongly support these efforts.
                                              [Para 8 l]
            3. The Committee expresses its happiness over the range of areas in which efforts are being made by the Department to
 develop immunodiagnostic kits. It emphasised that a set time frame be fixed for development of these kits. The Committee
 noted the progress made in the area of development of detection kit for kala azar, diagnostic test for detection of circulating
 antigen in human filariasis and HIV detection kits, etc; but felt strongly that the Department should be able to draw-up a time-
schedule by which the kits supported or developed by it would be available. DBT should, therefore, introduce pert charts for
 all the immunodiagnostic kits, as this would enable it to properly monitor the progress achieved in this area. The Committee
 fully appreciates the difficulties which one fates with regard to the development of biological systems; however, tight
 monitoring has to be introduced since development of low cost, easily used immunodiagnostic kits for common diseases is a
 priority area of DBT.
[9.1]
      4. The Committee is of the view that Indian scientists and Indian industry must try to obtain the best that is available
 out of modern biotechnological advances. It was noted that there is the Centre for Biochemicals, Delhi, which has been given
 the responsibility by DBT to start producing many recombinant agents, restriction enzymes, etc.; in addition there is the
 Bangalore based Gene, Lupin and many such industries which are now coming forward to produce these agents. In the view
 of the Committee DBT should obtain information on work done elsewhere in the world relating to biotechnology and the
 requirements for this work are not only for research but also for production in terms of chemicais and biologicals, of various

 technology from abroad. The efforts should be to have as much of these produced in the country since easy availability of
 these items of high quality underpin all developments in this field.                      [Para 10.1]

 immunodiagnostics, at a fairly early stage, both from the viewpoints of estimating market demand and from the viewpoint of

 that results have been successful at the laboratory scale, but when the industry comes into the picture, it requires larger
 quantity of input materials and the availability and costs of these become important. This can then change the whole scenario.

 and inputs required for production. It would be dearly desirable to bring in industry on an overlapping basis with the research

 Consortium Limited was created to bring an overlap between R&D on the one hand and production and trade on the other is
 indicative of this. The Committee would like the Department to strengthen this area further.

REPORT 
            The Department of Ocean Developm ent was created in July 1981 as a part of the Cabinet
Secretariat directly under the ch arge of the Prime Minister. Fr om March 1982, it became a separate
Department. In February 2006, it wa s notified as the Ministry of O cean Development. The Ministry o f
Earth Sciences has been created in July 2006 after merger of India Meteorological Department (IMD);
National Centre for Medium Range Weather For ecasting (NCMRWF); Indian  Institute of Tropical
Meteorology (IITM) and Earth Risk  Evaluation Centre (EREC) with  the then Ministry of Ocean
Development. The Ministry’s mandate is to lo ok after Atmospheric Sciences, Ocean Science & 
Technology and Seismology in an integrated manner. Ministry of Earth Sciences has been functioning
as a nodal Ministry for organising, c oordinating and promoting related Ea rth Sciences activities in the
country.  
  
2.         OCEAN SCIENCE 
2.1       The programmes pursued by the Ministry ove r the years have also kept  pace with developments 
world over and addressed na tional needs and prioriti es, in line with the Ocean Policy Statement o f 
1982.   
2.2       The programmes of the Ministry in the field of Ocean Science are directed towards: 
•
      Technology Development Programmes for future applications with  strategic, industrial and 
economic significance. 
•        Societal Programmes with direct/indirect benefit for the comm unity by technology applications
and pilot project demons tration with the participation of  the community for their socio-
economic prosperity, and for coastal area devel opment/management through scientific tools and 
techniques 
•        Marine Resource Programmes fo r exploration of marine li ving and non-living resources, 
techno-economic studies to evolve strategies for sustainable explorat ion and utilisation, an d
resource enhancement. 
•        Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions
with scientific and geo-political significance. 
•        Capacity Building Progr amme towards self-reliance through ba sic scientific re search in ocean 
sector, human resource develo pment and establishi ng Centres of Excel lence in academic 
institutions. 
•        Creation of public awareness of ocean, its potential and uses. 
  
3.         The scientific research and technol ogy development programmes are formulated, coordinate d
and executed through three autonomous institutions supported by the Ministry and two Attached offices
of the Ministry. These multi-disc iplinary and multi-institutional pr ogrammes are assisted by National
Research Laboratories, academic in stitutions and industries. Furthe r, Marine Research and Capacity
Building is one of the key programme areas of the Ministry to promote basic research in marine science

3.1              The oceanographic programmes have national, regional and global importance. With the
ratification of the UN C onvention on Law of the Sea,  a new international order has been established for
the oceans. India is represented in almost all the important  bodies on oceans. India will stand to benefit
enormously by provisions of  the convention, if we can build an integrated approa ch for scientific
planning, formulation, implementa tion and overall management  of the programmes with a
comprehensive organisational and institutional back up.  
3.2       The Ministry is the nodal agency for international programmes in  the ocean sector and 
representing the country in Inter-governmental  Oceanographic Commissi on (IOC) of UNESCO,
Regional Committee of IOC in Coastal Indian  Ocean (IOCINDIO), S outh Asian Regional Seas
Programme, Commission on th e Limits of Continental Shelf (CLC S), International Sea-Bed Authority 
(ISBA) and the State Parties of the United Nationa l Convention on the Law of the Seas (UNCLOS), the
Antarctic Treaty System (ATS) a nd its scientific and managerial organs – Commission on Conservation 
of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) , Council of Managers of National Antarctic
Programme (COMNAP), Scientific Committee on Anta rctic Research (SCAR), etc. These activities
have scientific, economic and geopol itical impacts. Hence, the activ ities of the Ministry address
Scientific Research and Technol ogy Development with or ientation towards a pplications, capacity
building and human resource development for self-re liance, and international programmes arising out of 
International obligations and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures. 
4.         ATMOSPHERIC SCIENCE  
4.1       The atmosphere plays a vital role in de fining the overall environmen t in which all organisms 
live. It impacts almost all kinds of human activities in a major way. Society has evolved in harmony
with the existing variability of weather and climate and needs the s upport of forecasts to manage many
of its critical functions.  Forecasting such a complex system as th e atmosphere is a growing science and
needs to be supported. Weather services in general have  very early origins in th is country and currently
engage the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the National Centre for Medium Range Weathe r
Forecasting (NCMRWF) which is a specialized agency for developing medium range forecast capability
in the country and the Indian In stitute of Tropical Meteorology (IIT M) which carries out research in
required areas.  
  
4.2       Advancement of the science in recent y ears indicate that a combined  approach involving land, 
oceanic and atmospheric processes holds the key to long and extende d range of forecasting which can
provide a credible policy tool. On the other hand, intensive monitoring and analysis of cloud systems
using Satellite and Radar technology can help us to accurately ga uge the severity of an immediately
impending calamity thereby prompting the selection of appropriate measures. Monitoring of earthquakes
issuing information about the location and intens ity of the earthquakes and hazard microzonation o f

18.       INDIA METEOROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT 
18.1     India Meteorological Department (IMD) is one of the oldest scientific institutions of the country. 
It is the national agency for providing weather foreca st & cyclone warnings. It is also the nodal agency
for monitoring seismic activities in the country.  The main objectives of the Department lie in: 
Forecasting and provision of climatological statisti cs for operational planning in various field o f
Agriculture, Aviation, Water Cons ervation, Oceanography, Industries, Astronomy etc. It maintains a
network of large number of obser vatories for acquisition of surf ace and upper air weather data. It
specifically issues weather forecast and ti mely disaster warning of severe weathe r
conditions/phenomena including cycl ones; provides adequate aviati on meteorological services fo r
efficient air navigation as per mandatory requirements; provides inputs to Flood Forecasts and
advisories to Agricultural Planners, Fishermen, Mountaineers etc.  
  
18.2     The IMD has a network for monitoring Seismic activity over th e territory of India for locating 
intensity and centers of earthquakes and to understa nd their processes & mechanisms.  It has a networ k 
for monitoring ozone, acid precipitation, atmospheri c aerosol and Radiation which are all important
environmental indicators.  
  
18.3     It has its own workshop for manufacturi ng equipments that are deployed in the basic
observational network and procures  specialized equipment required for sophisticated monitoring and
analysis. It is the nodal agency in the country fo r calibration and standardiz ing of several types o f
meteorological equipment. It carri es out and promotes research and development work in Atmospheric
and Meteorological Sciences and im parts meteorological training to  persons of developing countries
under WMO programmes and to Departmental, State Government and Defense services personnel. 
  
18.4     The total outlay for 2007-08 has been fixed at Rs 453.67 crores.  Since India Meteorological
Department (IMD) being the nodal Government agency in the country responsible for making 
systematic observations of weathe r and climate and providing weather related warnings/forecasts to all
sectors of activity, it is proposed to upgrade/modernize th e observational netw ork and modeling
capability.  
   
18.5     IMD prepared detailed Preliminary Fe asibility Report which wa s submitted to Planning
Commission in August, 04.  Planning Commission ga ve guide-lines for mode rnization of IMD and 
advised the newly created Ministry of Earth Sciences in May’ 2006 to review the w hole proposal and 
take a holistic view of the plan by integrating the observational re quirements for oceans  as well. The
