extreme situations that were beyond the control of the authority, the Executive should not be
permitted to supersede the authority as it might compromise with the transparency and functional
independence of the Authority.
21. One of the Members said that ‘public interest’ was a vague term and liable to be misused.
Allaying the fears, the Secretary replied that Clause 48 of the Bill was essentially for any
unforeseen situation.
22. It was suggested by the members that Authority needed to be strengthened. One of the
members of the committee wanted to know whether there was any dichotomy or not in a situation
when decision of the Appellate Authority was challenged in a court of law, replying to the query,
Secretary, DAE said that idea of keeping that provision was to place Council of nuclear safety at
a higher level in status compared to the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority.
23. It was suggested by one of the Members that as the decision were to be taken in the light
of scientific facts the search Committee was to be headed by a scientist rather than a High Court/
Supreme court judge. The Secretary clarified that reason behind representation of judiciary was to
make it a higher authority in status compared to NSRA.

1. Dr. A. Gopalakrishnan, Former Chairman, Atomic Energy Regulatory Board; and

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and Dr. Gopalakrishnan to the meeting
of the Committee and recollected that the Committee had earlier heard Dr. Gopalakrishnan on the
“Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Bill, 2010”. He requested Dr. Gopalakrishnan to add further to
his written suggestions that had already been circulated to Hon’ble Members and taken note by the
Committee.
93

94
3. Presenting his views before the Committee, Dr. Gopalakrishnan emphasised that there was
a close connection between the independence of the AERB and transparency to attain public safety.
He said that India was aspiring to move forward in the nuclear sector like all advanced countries
in the world and hence it was expected that we not  only emulated the technologies of other
countries but  also their practices in regulation. According to him, there was a serious dichotomy
between what was given in the Bill and what other countries like USA, Canada and France were
practicing. He further stated that the exact nature of practices in these countries might differ but
we should aim for the similar levels of transparency, independence and freedom of action but these
were totally missing from the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill. He added that the Authority
being created through this Bill would be a much more constrained and a much more captive
organisation of the Government even compared to AERB.
4. He said that broadly his comments on the Bill were in two areas – it was a question of
autonomy and independence on the one side and on the other side, it was lack of transparency and
openness. Commenting on the composition and functions of the proposed ‘Council of Nuclear
Safety’ he said that it was doubtful as to what extent, focused guidance required for safety of a
nuclear system which was highly technical and a techno-managerial affair would be available in
such a group. He added that looking at the subsequent actions of the Council, it was clear that
it would be used more as a controlling agent to keep the regulator in line. He, therefore, suggested
that this Council should be altered to be a Council on Civil Nuclear Policy. He suggested that the
Clause 7 of the Bill be changed to read as, “The Council of Civil Nuclear Policy shall frame and
establish policies and directions for the civilian nuclear activities in the country including matters
related to nuclear power and its safety and security. The Council shall oversee and support
autonomous functioning of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority and facilitate its independent
decision making in nuclear radiation and safety related matter”.
5. He appreciated that the Bill intended to create separate regulatory agencies for defence
related nuclear facilities which had hitherto been directly under the Department of Atomic Energy
and not under AERB. He, however, felt that it should be made clear as to which facilities Nuclear
Safety Regulatory Authority would be responsible for. He, therefore, suggested that the facilities
which were currently under the AERB’s purview and supervision, should be transferred to the
proposed Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority. He added that if civilian and defence facilities were
mixed together in a bucket and only one agency was looking after them, level of overall
transparency and openness would be reduced.
6. Thereafter, expressing his views on the appointment and removal of the Chairperson of the
NSRA, he suggested that after having completed the selection process, there was a - need to have
concurrence of Parliament on the lines of USA and Canada. When one of the Members pointed out
that, we did not have a system where appointment of Chairperson of various bodies was presented
to the Parliament for ratification and as such, this suggestion would entail a drastic change in the
system of governance in the country. To this, Dr. Gopalakrishnan averred that if it, seriously
violated practices and provisions in our Constitution, he would leave it to the Committee. However,
he asserted that his concern arose out of the fact that there seemed to be a certain level of
arbitrary power in the hands of the executive to appoint and remove the Chairman and Members
of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority.
7. Commenting on the explanation to Clause 20(1) of the Bill, he drew the attention of the
Committee to the words ‘The functions of the Authority shall, in no case, extend to the function
or any other matter which the Central Government was required to discharge under the Atomic
Energy Act, 1962’. He elaborated that it was .somewhat vague because setting up a new power
station, etc., came under the Atomic Energy Act and this provision basically debarred the Authority
to get involved in the safety aspect of the new facility. That was really not a workable preposition

95
because having created a Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority, the Authority should have the
freedom to examine and advise the Government on purchasing of new reactors or new systems.
He cited the example of Westinghouse Reactor, an American reactor, which was put through a 3
year detailed examination by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, because it was the first of its
kind reactor and they wanted it to be absolutely sure that it was safe and only after their clearance,
Government could buy that reactor.
8. He wanted to know as to why our regulator should not have the authority of looking at
the safety of system before they were purchased. When asked to clarify as to what exactly he
wanted to be included in the Bill, he stated that “In case the Operator or the Government intends
to introduce, install or commission a new, first of its kind nuclear facility system, a major sub-
system or component, which could potentially have serious safety-related adverse consequence,
shall be first subjected to a National Design Certification and preliminary safety approval by the
Authority before permission is granted for initiation of any associated site activity and facility
creation. Such a design certification and safety approval by the Authority shall be mandatory
notwithstanding any certifications or safety approvals granted by a foreign nuclear safety regulator
or Government”.
9. Commenting on Clause 20(2) (e) of the Bill regarding interaction of the Authority with
international organisations, etc., with prior approval of the Central Government, he was of the view
that the Authority should not directly interact with the foreign entities only on the policy related
matters and not on the technical matters. He, therefore, suggested to add policy related matters to
the proviso of Clause 20(2) (e).
10. Submitting his view on Clause 20(2)(q) of the Bill, he stated that it was somewhat vague to
put the onus on the Authority that it should discharge its powers and functions consistent with
international obligations of India. With such a provision, questioning any international obligation
from the safety point of view could become difficult. He, therefore, gave the following suggestions
to modify Clause 20(2)( q) “the operator shall bring to the attention of the Authority any
international obligation or treaty, which they, or, the Government are likely to enter into or have
entered into, and, the Authority shall then examine the consequences thereof from the stand point
of impact of acceding to that obligation the safety of the public and the environment. Once the
Authority completes this assessment, it shall advise the Government of their comprehensive views
in writing on the safety consequences of having entered into or entering into such international
obligation. Thereafter, the Authority shall discharge its functions as directed by the Government.
However, in case, the Authority considers that the final Government decision is not in the best
interest of public safety, health and environment, the authority shall prepare and place on record
their dissenting note before the Council with a request to forward the same to both Houses of
Parliament and include the same in their Annual Report”.
11. However, the Committee felt that the above suggestions would set a precedent for others
at various levels and it would be an unending process with other organisations also coming up with
similar demands. Intervening in the matter, National Security Advisor stated that the assumptions
on which the discussion was being held, was not true. He made it clear that before entering into
any agreement with foreign countries, three conditions were made very clear. Firstly, that they
would have to be competitive with other sources of energy in India, secondly, that they could not
sell reactors which had not been certified in their respective countries and thirdly that the reactor
would go through our regulatory procedures and safety procedures. So the assumption through out
in all the agreements was that in India, the law of India applied.
12. On Clauses 21 and 42 of the Bill, he wondered how an Authority selected by a selection
committee appointed by a Council headed by the Prime Minister and senior Cabinet Ministers could
be indecent and would single handedly overthrow the sovereignty and integrity of India. He was

96
of the view that these two Clauses were superfluous and did not add any value to the Act. He,
therefore, suggested that these Clauses should be dropped. Commenting further on Clause 42, he
added that it was not clear in the Bill on which aspect Government felt the necessity to give
directions to the Authority. He suggested inclusion of two Clauses in the Bill ill case Government
felt it necessary to retain Clause 42 in the Bill. His suggestions read as follows:
(i) In case the Authority, upon a thorough evaluation of the implications of following a
Government directive, finds no potential adverse impact could arise on public safety or
environment, they may document the entire matter and proceed with implementing the
Government directive.
(ii) If they found that unacceptable and adverse impact could thereby arise on public
safety or the environment, the Authority shall document the entire matter along with

reconsideration of the directive given by the Government. The Authority shall prepare
a dissent note and then submit it to them.
13. National Security Advisor clarified that the need to give direction came from the incident
of radiation leak at Mayapuri, when the Government felt that it had to ask Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board (AERB) not only to look into the incident but also to devise an operating
procedure and do a census of all radiation sources, etc. The purpose, therefore, was positive and
it was not to tell the AERB not to do this or that. Former Chairman, AERB, however, asserted that
the directives for morality, decency, public interest, etc. should be dropped from Clauses 21 and

15. Emphasizing on the need for transparency and openness, he suggested three areas where
we could improve. One area was putting such information on the website on which considered
decision had been taken like minutes of the meeting or summaries of the action taken, summary

were given to  the public to  put questions face to  face and these were answered after giving them
certain written material and the third aspect was creation of small local level committees having
representatives, from Panchayats, local college professors, etc., which would meet at least once
in three months and interact with the local people.

REPORT
Nuclear technology is perhaps one of the most contentious and controversial technologies
in the world which, notwithstanding the fact that this is highly useful and beneficial for the people,
has not got the credit it deserves. It is notorious for its potential to cause devastating and
catastrophic consequences, lesser known as source of clean and green energy and very little
known for its useful applications in the field of health, agriculture, industry and basic research.
2. Evolution of atomic energy programme in India can be traced back to 1948 when Atomic
Energy Commission was set up for formulation of policies and direction of the programmes in the
country. To implement its policies and programmes, the Department of Atomic Energy came into
being on 3
rd August, 1954 with Dr. Bhabha, the Father of Nuclear Programme in India, as its
Secretary. The atomic energy programme in our country which was initiated in a modest manner with
the objective of peaceful uses of atomic energy to meet our energy requirements, has now grown
manifold and has become multi-dimensional and multi-disciplinary in nature. Besides power
production, development of non-power applications of nuclear technology for use in agriculture,
healthcare, industry, water, food preservation, radiation processing of material, care for environment,
isotope hydrology, etc. for societal benefits is being undertaken in an emphatic manner. The first
commercial nuclear power programme began in 1969 with the operation of Tarapur Atomic Power
Station and currently Atomic Energy caters to about 3 per cent of the country’s total energy demand.
The Department has, over the years, evolved a broad-based organisation consisting of 6 Research &
Development Centres, 5 Public Sector Undertakings, 3 Industrial Organisations, 3 Service
Organisations and 9 Aided Institutions. Besides, through Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences
(BRNS) and National Board of Higher Mathematics, Department of Atomic Energy promotes research
in nuclear and allied fields and mathematics respectively. There are two deemed Universities under the
ambit of the Department of Atomic Energy, namely, Homi Bhabha National Institute and Tata Institute
of Fundamental Research. Academic Programmes are run by 4 Research & Development Units, viz.
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Mumbai; Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research
(IGCAR), Kalpakkam; Raja Ramanna Centre for Advance Technology (RRCAT), Indore; Variable
Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC), Kolkata and 6 Grants-in-Aid Institutions viz. Saha Institute of
Nuclear Physics (SINP), Kolkata; Institute of Physics (IOP), Bhubaneswar; Institute for Plasma
Research (IPR), Gandhi Nagar; Institute of Mathematical Science (IIMSC), Chennai; Harishchandra
Research Institute (HRI), Allahabad and Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), Mumbai under the umbrella of
the Homi Bhabha National Institute. Academic programmes of National Institute of Science Education
and Research (NISER), an Autonomous Body under the Department of Atomic Energy are also
conducted under the aegis of Homi Bhabha National Institute. Academic Programmes include Ph.D,
Integrated Ph.D., M.Tech., M.Phil., M.Sc. (Engineering) and Post Graduate Diploma in all science
and engineering disciplines, etc.
3. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS OF THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY
3.1 Demands for Grants for Department of Atomic Energy are made under Demand No. 4 &
Demand No. 5. Demand No. 4 consists of such sectors of Atomic Energy as Research &
Development, Industries and Minerals while Demand No. 5 comprises of Nuclear Power Schemes.
6 Research Centres, 3 Industrial Organisations, 3 Service Organisations and 3 Public Sector
Undertakings fall within the ambit of the Demand No. 4 while 2 Public Sector Undertakings,
namely, Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) and Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam
Ltd. (BHA VINI) fall within Demand No. 5. The total budgetary outlay for the Department of Atomic

4.8 When the Committee enquired from the Department the reasons for allocated funds
remaining unutilized during the Financial Year 2010-11 and 2011-12, the factors enumerated by the
Department were mostly of administrative nature. For example, explaining the reasons for less
expenditure in 2010-11, the Department stated that the funds remained unutilized in Research &
Development Sector, mainly due to delay in procurement of machinery and equipments for the
projects of BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC, etc.; delay in award of contract for new campus of
BARC; late receipt of clearance of Ministry of Environment and Forests for construction activities,
etc. Under Industry Sector, the reasons for less expenditure varied from delay in projects of
Nuclear Recycle Group; delay in construction work of housing project for Heavy Water Plant,
Manuguru; delay in sanction of Fast Breeder Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility Project, etc. Under Mineral
Sector, underutilization of allocated funds was stated to be mainly due to delay in sanction of
Uranium Corporation of India Ltd. Projects. Similarly, under Power Sector, the main reasons for
underutilization was the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor Project which encountered technological
difficulties during manufacture and assembly together with delay in finalization of orders due to
non-availability of suppliers. Reasons for underutilization under various sectors of the Department
during the year 2011-12 are no different from the reasons given for the underutilization of funds
for the year 2010-11. The Department stated that under Research & Development Sector funds
remained unutilized due to delay in infrastructure projects of TIFR, BARC and project of
International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) and Global Centre for Nuclear Energy
Partnership. Under Industry Sector, the reasons were delay in receipt of sanction for Fast Breeder
Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility etc., while, under Mineral Sector, delay in sanction of UCIL Projects,
inter-alia, was the main reason for non-utilisation of allocation. Slow progress of Prototype Fast
Breeder Reactor project, mainly contributed to the underutilization of allocated resources under
Power Sector.
4.9 On an analysis of the above reasons, the Committee finds that the grounds given by the
Department for underutilization of allocated funds are mainly of administrative nature and feels that
these could have been overcome by the Department by acting in an efficient, effective and
professional manner. It is also constrained to observe that the reasons which led to underutilization
of funds during the year 2010-11 have been allowed to persist even in the year 2011-12 and it is
only the Department which is to be held responsible for not addressing those issues in right
earnest. The Committee does not seem inclined to be convinced by the reasons given by the
Department and feels that the resources which are allocated to the Department are very scarce and

7
a scientific Department like Atomic Energy must make full use of these resources. Blocking or not
utilizing the scarce resource some how affects overall development of the country as these
resources could very well have been earmarked for the other welfare schemes/projects for the
people of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Financial Year 2012-13,
being the first Financial Year of the XII Five Year Plan, the Department must ensure that
the allocation made to the Department is fully utilized not only during the current year but
also throughout the entire Plan period.
4.10 The Committee was, however, informed that reduced allocation of Non-Plan expenditure
in Demand No. 4 to the extent of Rs. 984.67 Crores, if not restored would affect the production
of Heavy Water and Nuclear fuel besides affecting O&M of various R&D units of the
Department. Similarly, the shortfall of Rs. 377.94 Crores in Demand No. 5, if not restored will
affect the import of nuclear fuel. The Committee takes note of adverse consequences arising
from drastic cut in the Non-Plan allocation under Demand No. 4 & 5 and recommends that Non-
Plan allocation be suitably enhanced at R.E. stage to avoid adverse impact arising from reduction
of Non-Plan allocation.
4.11 The Committee feels that one of the main reasons behind underutilization of allocated
resources is lack of effective and strict monitoring mechanism to review the progress of its on
going schemes/programmes from time to time. The Committee had, in its 207
th Report on Demands
for Grants 2010-11 of the Department of Atomic Energy expressed its serious concern over the
underutilization of funds under different sectors despite an elaborate and comprehensive monitoring
mechanism adopted by the Department and had recommended that the Department needed to
further strengthen the mechanism for monitoring of ongoing schemes for their effective
implementation and elimination of any scope of surrender of funds at a later date due to non-
utilisation/underutilization. The Department had in its Action Taken Note claimed that the monitoring
mechanisms developed by the Department are being effectively used to eliminate the scope of
shortage or surrender of funds at later stage. It had further informed that the recommendations of
the Committee had been brought to the notice of all Head of Constituent Units/Autonomous Bodies
and Public Sector Undertakings of the Department and also to all Members concerned with the
monitoring mechanisms with a request that all necessary efforts were taken at their end to further
strengthen the monitoring system to achieve full utilisation of Plan Funds. However, the Committee
finds that the trend of utilisation in all the 4 Sectors for the year 2011-12, shows that the

4.19 RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT CENTRES
4.20 Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)
4.20.1 Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, which is almost synonymous with the atomic energy
programme of our country is an internationally renowned multidisciplinary and multi-scale activity
research & development organisation engaged in comprehensive research & development
programmes aimed at harnessing nuclear energy and its utility for the benefit of the society. Some
of the prominent activities of BARC include entire spectrum of fuel – cycle activities, developing
futuristic nuclear reactors, fabricating nuclear fuels, reprocessing of spent fuel, waste management,
robotics, super computers, lasers, accelerators, human genomes, nanotechnology, super-
conductivity, etc. BARC is also actively involved in developing applications of radiation technologies
for the purpose of food preservation, radiation mutation breeding of varieties of pulses, groundnuts
and other seeds, radio isotopes for healthcare, trouble shooting in industries, etc. While, its main
campus is located at Mumbai, it has other campuses at Tarapur, Kalpakkam and Mysore and a new
campus is being set up at Visakhapatnam.
4.20.2 BARC was allocated an amount of Rs. 2554.00 crores both Plan and Non-Plan at B.E. level
for the year 2011-12. However, it could utilize Rs. 2408.00 crores at the R.E. level, thus, showing
an underutilization of Rs. 146.00 crores. When the Committee enquired about the reasons for
underutilization of allocated outlay, the Department of Atomic Energy came out with the plea that
the provision of Rs. 80 crores for composite contract for development of facilities at Atchutapuram
Mandal – Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh could not be utilized as it had to be retendered, Micro
Nano Engineering Initiative, could not be taken up, construction of New Engineering Halls at
Visakhapatnam Campus of BARC remained pending for want of approval of Department of Atomic
Energy, provision for Establishment of Infrastructural Facility and Production Capacities at Rare
Materials Plant (RMP), Mysore was reduced by Rs. 40.00 crores keeping in view the status of
ongoing composite contracts and the provision made for setting up of Uranium Oxide facility at
Kalpakkam was reduced by Rs. 30 crores due to slow progress of the work. The Committee finds
that all these grounds cited by the Department are of routine administrative nature which could
have been avoided by the Department as delay in completion of infrastructure projects leads to time
and cost overrun and affects research & development work. The Committee feels that it is a
matter of concern that as against the B.E. allocation of Rs. 1190.00 crores under Plan Head,
BARC could utilize only Rs. 1015.00 crores, thus, leaving a gap of Rs. 175.00 crores. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that these sort of loopholes which lead to
underutilization of funds should be plugged in future.
4.20.3 The allocation for BARC for the year 2012-13 has been increased by Rs. 68.70 crores in
comparison to the B.E. allocation for the year 2011-12. While, the increase as against the R.E.
allocation for the year 2011-12 amounts to Rs. 214.70 crores. The Committee was informed
that the increase in provision for the year 2012-13 is mainly for the development of
facilities at BARC, Visakhapatnam and for setting up of integrated nuclear projects at
Tarapur. The Committee is happy to note that allocation for BARC, a prestigious research
& development institution, has been increased notwithstanding its poor performance in
terms of financial achievements. It however, recommends all out efforts be made to fully
utilize the outlay and that no excuse whatsoever should be allowed to come in its way.
4.20.4 The Committee is happy to note that BARC is actively pursuing research in nuclear
agriculture by using genetic mutation of crop plants using ionizing radiation aimed at
improved yields, resistant to disease which has resulted in production of several new crop
varieties. Over 38 new crop varieties produced by BARC have thus far been released for
use by farmers. The mutant of black gram produced by BARC accounts for more than 90

11
per cent of its cultivation in Maharashtra. The Committee feels that research in nuclear
agriculture pursued by the Department of Atomic Energy is all the more relevant in today’s
context when the phenomena of climate change has started making its impact on
agricultural yields. The Committee, however, feels that the efforts made by the Department,
thus far, in this direction are not enough to meet the challenges posed before us. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should intensify its efforts in
developing more and more high yielding disease resistant crop varieties not only of pulses,
groundnuts, etc., but also of cereals like wheat and rice.
4.20.5 The Committee is also of the view that there is need for popularizing new high
yielding varieties developed at BARC, so that benefit of research done at BARC reaches all
nooks and corners of the country and does not remain restricted only to farmers of
Maharashtra. The Committee recommends that Department chalk out a popularization cum
awareness campaign to make people throughout the country aware of various varieties
developed at BARC and for popularizing them.
4.20.6 The Committee also understands that the Department is actively engaged in developing
technologies for societal benefits which include prevention of post-harvest losses of foodgrains,
vegetables, fruits, seafood, etc.; handling enormous amount of waste generated; treatment of
municipal sewage, etc.
4.20.7 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should create a
separate agency of its own instead of depending on other agencies for popularizing and
marketing of socially beneficial technologies like Nisargruna Biogas Plant for handling
biodegradable wastes; Sludge Hygienization Research Irradiation (SHRI) for treatment of
municipal sewage, etc. including its technology on food preservation, nuclear medicine and
healthcare, so that, the benefit ultimately could reach the society at large.
4.21 Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), Kalpakkam
4.21.1 IGCAR, an internationally known research centre for nuclear science & technology, is the
second largest Research and Development centre of the Department of Atomic Energy after BARC.
The design and development of liquid sodium cooled Fast Breeder Reactors alongwith associated
fuel cycle technologies is the main mandate of the Centre. The Centre has also been pursuing basic
research in frontier areas of science & technology.
4.21.2 An increase of Rs. 431.30 crores has been made for IGCAR as against the Budget
Estimates of the last year. When the Committee asked the reasons for increase in allocation this
year, while the Centre failed to utilize Rs. 121.72 crores out of the budgetary allocation of
Rs. 711.70 crores made last year as the Revised Estimates remained at Rs. 589.98 crores, the

project in industry sector viz. Fast Reactor Fuel Cycle facility. Responding to the reasons for
under-utilisation of Rs. 121.72 crores last year, the Department stated that it was on account of
delay in receipt of approval for the Fast Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility Project.
4.21.3 The Committee understands that receipt/grant of approval for the project is purely an
internal matter of the Department which could have been sorted out well in time. The Committee
does not find it to be a convincing cause for spill over of a project from one financial year to
the other and hence expresses its serious concern over such lame excuses. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the process of receipt/grant approval for projects for which
allocation has been earmarked must be completed in the same financial year, so that, the
allocated outlay are fully utilized in that year itself. The Committee also expresses its
serious concern over such sort of delay for a matter and crucial project like fast reactor

12
fuel cycle facility which is badly required for the second stage nuclear power programme
and recommends that such procedural delays should not be allowed to come in the way of
such an important programme in future.
4.22 Raja Rama nna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT), Indore
4.22.1 RRCAT is yet another research & development Centre which is mainly engaged in
development of particle accelerators and lasers alongwith their applications. It is also pursuing R&D
programmes in advanced technologies like cryogenics, ultra high vacuum super conducting cavities
and magnets. A helium liquefier has been indigenously developed by the Centre for the first time

Nuclear Research (SERN), Geneva and FERMILAB, USA.
4.22.2 The total budgetary outlay at B.E. stage for this Centre last year was Rs. 248.15 crores

outstanding performance in utilisation of funds last year, the Department explained that the
reduction is mainly on account of keeping minimum requirement for the new projects of Twelfth

4.23.1 VECC is a premier institute of the country for research in nuclear science in the field of

13
this year but also accomplish the task of development of software for hearing impaired and
medical cyclotron project within the stipulated targeted period.
4.23.4 Research & development is key to innovation of a path breaking technology. It being capital
intensive requires allocation of adequate resources to achieve the desired objective. But apart from
money what counts is the time within which a technology developed is put in commercial domain
since it is a highly competitive age where all capable countries are vying with one another to take
the lead. As such, mere completion of a mission is not enough. What matters most is how soon
the technology makes its presence felt in the market. The Committee finds that out of the total
approved outlay both plan & outlay for the year 2012-13 of Rs. 19983.01 crores only an amount
of Rs. 2946.83 crores (Plan Head) has been earmarked for Research & Development. Further,
Government has allocated only Rs. 2946.83 crores for research & development under Plan Head
as against the projected demand of Rs. 3035.39 crores this year. While the Committee appreciates
the efforts being put in by our scientists engaged in research & development, it feels that the
business as usual approach would not do. The time has come when our scientists/ scientific
departments should gear up full throttle not only to a lead in cutting edge technologies but to realize
and redeem the dreams of converting scientific knowledge into technology for use in commercial
domain. The Committee, therefore, recommends that accomplishment of third stage nuclear
power programme using thorium as fuel for power generation on commercial basis, research
on Compact High Temperature Reactor (CHTR) and on Hydrogen energy needs to be
intensified and results achieved in a time bound manner.
4.24 MINERAL SECTOR
4.25 Uranium Corporation of India Ltd. (UCIL)
4.25.1 UCIL is a Pubic Sector Undertaking of the Department of Atomic Energy whose specific
mandate is mining and processing of Uranium ore to produce Uranium concentrate for nuclear
power generation. To attain the above objective UCIL is engaged in design & construction of
underground mines, ore processing and other related activities.
4.25.2 Supply and availability of Uranium forms a critical component of expansion of nuclear
power programme of our country. Non-availability of fuel owing to shortage of Uranium continues
to be a major constraint in enhancing nuclear energy production. Worse, operation of PHWRs
fuelled with domestic Uranium is not able to attain full capacity factor. As per the Annual Report
– 2011-12 of the Department, the reactors operating with domestic fuel supply registered capacity
factor of about 67 per cent till December 31, 2011. However, the Committee is surprised to note
that out of B.E. allocation of Rs. 154.00 crores for the year 2011-12, UCIL under Major Head 4861
and Rs. 487.00 crores under Major Head 12861 was drastically reduced at R.E. stage to only
Rs. 25.00 and Rs. 274.00 crores respectively apparently due to non-utilisation or underutilization
of funds by UCIL. When the Committee enquired about the reasons for gross utilisation of funds
by UCIL, it was informed that it was due to delay in sanctioning of the Tummalapalle Expansion
Project and Uranium Project at Gogi. The Committee understands that sanctioning of the project
is an internal matter of the Department, which could have been obtained in time as such a vital
project on which expansion of nuclear power programme so heavily depends cannot be made to
suffer due to procedural reasons. The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over such
a lackadaisical approach of the Department.
4.25.3 The allocation for Uranium Corporation India Ltd. for this year under Major Head 4861 has
been increased from Rs. 154.00 crores B.E. last year to Rs. 216.00 crores this year, but under
Major Head 12861, it has been slightly reduced from Rs. 487.00 crores to Rs. 467.00 crores. The
Department has stated that the provision has been made in anticipation of sanction of the

14
Tummalapalle Expansion Project and Uranium Project at Gogi and also the new projects envisaged
under Twelfth Plan. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgetary allocation made
this year must be fully utilized and the Department should not come out with procedural excuses
next year. The Committee also recommends that the new potential heavy mineral zones identified
by Atomic Minerals Directorate in new areas must also be exploited so as to extract as much
Uranium ore as possible and for this purpose, the Department should prepare a time bound Action
Plan.
4.25.4 The Committee also expresses its serious concern over the fact that the Lambapur Project,
Nalgunda District, Andhra Pradesh and Kylleng Pyndengsotiong Mawthabah (KPM), West Khalsi
Hills District, Meghalaya, which are being pursued from Tenth Five Year Plan onwards have not
yet been set up owing to resistance by the local people. The Committee understands that large
amount of money has already been spent on these Projects. The Committee fails to understand as
to why for so long the Department has not been able to amicably sort out the problems with the
local people. The Committee feels that the concern of the people about health hazard posed by
Uranium mining needs to be allayed with extensive public awareness and outreach programmes
instead of standing firm on the notion that Uranium mining does not pose any health hazards and
a number of health surveys conducted confirm this fact. The fact that Uranium mining does not
cause health hazard needs to be appropriately conveyed to the people so as to convince them and
win their confidence. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
pay due attention on the above observations of the Committee.
4.26 Atomic Minerals Directorate, for exploration and Research (AMD)
4.26.1 AMD, a research & development centre of the Department carry out survey, prospecting
and exploration of atomic minerals and its activities include assessment, analysis, evolution,
characterization and categorization of atomic minerals, design and fabrication of radiometric survey
instruments, etc. AMD also plays a role in nuclear power programme by carrying out site selection
for nuclear power reactors and waste disposals. During the year, 2010-11, AMD through its
exploration activities has established over 962 tonnes of additional reserves of Uranium Oxides in
Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Meghalaya and Jharkhand. AMD continue its survey and exploration
activities along the coastal tracks of Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and
Karnataka and identified new potential heavy mineral zones. This year outlay for Atomic Minerals
Division is Rs. 261.07 crores as against B.E. 2011-12 of Rs. 288.87 crores. A shortfall of
Rs. 27.80 crores has been made in comparison to the last year B.E. allocation. Explaining the
reasons of the shortfall, the Department stated that it was due to completion of the Project called
“Augmentation of Airborne and Ground Geophysical Capabilities”. It was further stated that during
Twelfth Plan, an outlay of Rs. 112.00 crores only is envisaged under this Project as against
Eleventh Plan outlay of Rs. 276.00 crores.
4.26.2 The Committee, although satisfied with the explanation given by the Department for the
shortfall in the allocation, feels that Atomic Minerals Directorate which is shouldering the
responsibility of identifying mineral resources for the nuclear power programme should continue to
intensify its survey and exploration activities, so that, the country could strive to attain, as far as
possible, self-dependents in Uranium. The Committee, therefore, recommends that AMD should
make efforts to cover those areas of the country to identify prospective mineral resources
which have been left untouched so far.
4.27 T ata Memorial Centre (TMC)
4.27.1 TMC is an autonomous body under the Department of Atomic Energy which sets standards
of therapy for treatment modalities of cancer. It also works as a centre which imparts training to

15
doctors, scientists and para-medical staff in the field. Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research
and Education Cancer (ACTREC) at Navi Mumbai is one of its units which conducts basic,
community based and clinically oriented research on multiple facets of cancer, particularly, the
cancer of Oral Cavity, Cervix, Leukemia and Lymphomas and tobacco related cancers which are
prevalent in India. This Centre is running several programmes like, mobile cancer screening, TMC
– Rural Outreach Programme, TMC – Urban Outreach Programme, Cancer and public health
research, basic and translational cancer research, National Cancer Grid upgradation for development
of apex cancer institute in each zone of the country for facilitating uniformity in criteria, for
prevention, early diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients suffering from Cancer.
4.27.2 The Committee feels that Cancer is emerging as a major deadly disease in our country and
adequate infrastructure facilities for its early detection, effective and economical treatment need to be
created on priority basis. This assumes importance also because the poor cannot afford to get
treatment, its cost being exorbitantly high. The Committee, therefore, feels that TMC can play a lead
role in achieving the above objectives and for this purpose it is imperative that it expands its network
in other major cities and various States. During its visit to Tata Memorial Hospital, Mumbai, the
Committee found that the Hospital was over crowded with patients mainly because of the lack of
economical and effective treatment facilities elsewhere. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that TMC should, in a time bound manner, try to establish its Centres in other parts of the
country with high cancer case rates. Simultaneously, it should also makes sincere efforts to
develop tertiary level cancer care facilities in each State/Region, so that, patients need not
travel from remote and far flung areas all the way to Mumbai. The Committee also
recommends that adequate financial allocation should be provided to the Centre, so that, it
could not only undertake research in the field of cancer, but also expand its activities and
reach in different parts of the country. The Committee expresses its displeasure over the
reduction of allocation for the Centre in B.E. 2012-13 which is Rs. 248.15 crores as against
the B.E. Rs. 289.78 crores last year and recommends that adequate budgetary support needs
to be provided to the Centre so that it is able to cater to the needs of the cancer patients,
especially the poor through expansion and outreach programmes.
4.28 Aided Institutions/Autonomous Bodies
4.28.1 Human resource with high degree of excellence, competence and expertise is the key to
development of cutting edge technologies and for grooming and nurturing such talent human
resource academic institutions are necessary. For this purpose, Department of Atomic Energy has
a network of eight Autonomous Bodies and one Education Society, fully funded by the Department.
Budgetary allocations to these Autonomous Bodies are made under the Head “Autonomous Bodies”.
4.28.2 The Committee notes that out of the total B.E. allocation of Rs. 1204.63 Crores under this
Head last year, an amount of Rs. 990.39 Crores has been utilized resulting in underutilization of
Rs. 214.29 crores. When the Committee asked about the reasons for the underutilization, it was
explained that the amount of Rs. 109.00 crores could not be utilized by Institute of Plasma
Research as International organisation has not released the design of the International
Thermonuclear Experimental Reactors delaying payments for the same. Further, an amount of
Rs. 18.00 crores could not be used due to delay in sanction for the project – New Campus for
Fusion Reactor Related Activities. Tata Institute of Fundamental Research failed to utilize an amount
of Rs. 91.80 crores due to delay in obtaining statutory permission for infrastructure facilities, TIFR
New Campus Development, etc.
4.28.3 The Committee expresses its concern over underutilization of funds by these prominent
institutions as it would adversely affect our preparations/advancement in the field of nuclear
science.

16
4.28.4 The Committee is hopeful that the Department would give due consideration to the
recommendations of the Committee and take all necessary measures to obviate the
possibilities of underutilization of funds under various schemes.
4.29 POWER SECTOR
4.30. Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (BHAVINI)
4.30.1 BHA VINI is a public sector undertaking under the Department of Atomic Energy. It was
incorporated in October, 2003 to plan, execute and operate an integrated programme of Fast
Breeder Technology based nuclear power plants for generating electricity on a commercial basis
commencing with Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam. The authorised share capital of
BHA VINI is Rs. 5000 crores. Construction of Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor, sanctioned cost of
which was Rs. 3492 crores and later revised upto Rs. 5677 crores with the expected completion
by September 2014 is in advanced stage.
4.30.2 The current year budgetary allocation including IEBR for BHA VINI is Rs. 700 crores as
against the Budget Estimates of the last year, which was Rs. 1025.00 crores resulting in a
reduction of Rs. 325.00 crores. The Department justified the reduction by stating that the reduction
is commensurate with the actual requirement of funds as the project was nearing its completion.
As regards physical progress, the target could not be achieved in any of the financial years of the
Eleventh Five Year Plan starting from the year 2007-08 to 2011-12.

4.30.4 A cursory glance of the above statement indicates that except for the year 2008-09 and
2009-10, the target of financial progress could not be achieved in the year 2007-08, 2010-11 and
2011-12. In the year, 2010-11, the state of financial progress was such that out of an allocation
of Rs. 1275 crores, only Rs. 330 crores could be utilized. As against physical progress target of
45 per cent in 2007-08, 57 per cent in 2008-09, 67 per cent in 2009-10, 75 per cent in 2010-
11 and 90 per cent in 2011-12, the actual target achieved remained at 35, 45, 56, 70, and 82 per-
cent (achieved upto February, 2012) respectively.
4.30.5 The Committee feels that a department like Atomic Energy is expected to be more
disciplined particularly in planning and execution of projects and hence slippage of target both
physical and financial reflects adversely on the overall performance of the Department. The
Committee also notes that setting up of Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor, the second stage of the
Indian Nuclear Power Programme is crucial for the commencement of the third stage nuclear
power programme for thorium utilisation. The Committee also notes that the target of achieving
three stage nuclear power programme leading ultimately to development of thorium fuel based
reactors has already been delayed considerably and to meet the ever increasing demand of energy,
we need to accelerate growth of installed capacity of nuclear power projects with indigenous
technology using domestic fuel. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should make all out efforts to make the prototype fast breeder reactor operational by
targeted date of completion, i.e., September, 2014 and start its commercial operation by
2014-15 as scheduled.
4.30.6 Atomic energy, still not playing its due role in meeting the increasing energy requirements
of the country, is an area of concern which needs to be addressed sooner. It becomes all the more
inevitable as it is a low carbon emission technology, a technology very badly needed for sustainable
development. At present, Nuclear Power Corporation India Ltd. is operating 20 Nuclear Power
Reactors at six locations with a total installed capacity of 4780 Mw. The proposed capacity addition
target during the Twelfth Five Year Plan is envisaged as 5300 Mw. Thus by the end of Twelfth
Plan, the nuclear power capacity is expected to reach 10080 Mw. The total capacity is expected
to reach the target of 21520 Mw by the end of Thirteenth Five Year Plan and, 27660 Mw by
2023-24 by progressive completion of all the proposed projects.
4.30.7 However, the above target is subject to availability of indigenous fuel for Pressurized Heavy
Water Reactors, Prototype Fast Breeder Reactors being made operational and materialization of
international cooperation. In view of international cooperation for Light Water Reactors taking
longer time than envisaged and establishment of fuel linkages, Eleventh Plan nuclear power
production proposals had to be revisited. Out of the targeted capacity addition of 3160 Mw during
Eleventh Plan only 880 Mw could be added till 2010-11.
4.30.8 While the Committee appreciates the NPCIL motto of ‘Safety first and production next’ and
also the constraints the Department is facing both domestic and international, it feels that the time
has come when the Department must enhance its nuclear energy capacity in a big way to help the
country sustain its economic growth. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department must not leave any stone unturned to ensure that nuclear power generation
capacity is given a big boost as the country cannot afford any laxity on this front any more.

1. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Financial Year 2012-13, being the first
Financial Year of the Twelfth Five Year Plan, the Department must ensure that the
allocation made to the Department is fully utilized not only during the current year but also
throughout the entire Plan period. (Para 4.9)
2. The Committee takes note of adverse consequences arising from drastic cut in the
Non-Plan allocation under Demand No. 4 & 5 and recommends that Non-Plan allocation be
suitably enhanced at R.E. stage to avoid adverse impact arising from reduction of Non-Plan
allocation. (Para 4.10)

ensure full utilisation of funds and, therefore, recommends that the monitoring mechanism
needs to be so strengthened and revamped as to preclude any possibility of underutilization/
non-utilisation of allocated funds on almost similar grounds year after year. (Para 4.14)

11. The Chairman after welcoming Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy and his team of
officials to the meeting of the Committee informed that the Committee proposed to discuss the
functioning and Demand for Grants of the Department for the year 2012.
12. Expressing happiness over the growth of nuclear power generation by 39 per cent in the
year 2011 as compared to the previous year Chairman mentioned that with several reactors under
construction share of nuclear power in total power generation would rise, significantly in years to
come.
13. Thereafter, Chairman desired to know the future roadmap drawn by the Department to
augment share of nuclear power to rid the country of chronic power shortage. Secretary was also
asked to apprise the Committee of the results of stress test undertaken in the wake of Fukushima
incident and the steps taken to ensure full safety of nuclear power reactors. He was also asked
to appraise the Committee of the new applications of atomic energy in the fields of agriculture,
food technology and healthcare, thrust areas of the Department for the XII Five Year Plan and
Financial Year 2012-13, budgetary allocations made for the year 2012-13, targets set for the year
and whether the allocations are sufficient to carry out the programmes/schemes and if not, detailed
justification for the increased allocation. Thereafter, Chairman asked the Secretary to start his
presentation.
14. The Secretary, first of all, thanked the Committee for the opportunity given to the
Department to present the work done by the Department. Thereafter, he made a power point
presentation. Intervening during the power point presentation, the Committee enquired about the
achievements, aims and objectives of Tata Memorial Centre (TMC). Director, TMC informed the
Committee that the primary aim of TMC was to give cost effective treatment to cancer patients.
He informed that while the cost of the medicine that came from the West for treatment of cancer,
TMC has formulated medicines and interventions which could give the same kind of benefits at the

25
cost of Rs. 100 only. Secondly, the Centre provided radiation therapy at a cost which was 50 per
cent of the cost of any other treatment available in the market. TMC had made yet another
achievement by documentation of the cancers which were contributing to death in our country,
according to which 40 per cent of death was tobacco related, 25 per cent infection related and
another 25 per cent was related to obesity.
15. Responding to the issues raised by Chairman, the Secretary, on the safety aspect of nuclear
power reactors, emphasised that the Department gave maximum emphasis on safety in terms of
new design, in terms of running a plant and continuously monitoring the parameters to see that
a nuclear power reactor was always in safe operation. He further added that now there would be
an international review of the safety issues. India would become a member of the Operation
Science and Advisory Team (OSAT) of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and this agency
would submit their report  to the Government and to the regulator and not to the operator. This
report would also be made public. Several reviews initiated in the wake of Fukushima disaster
unequivocally prove that all of the system in our nuclear power reactors are in perfect order. AERB
has also constituted a separate Committee to assess the safety features of different types of
reactors. AERB had suggested some new safety measures which are being implemented. Secretary
further added that Fukushima disaster occurred as the decay heat could not be taken out of the
reactor. For instance, if it was a 100  mw reactor, after complete shutdown, it would be producing
about 1 mw and hence the heat thus developed had to be taken out. To take the heat out normally,
we had power supplies of 4 different categories, i.e., from category 1 to 4, but if all the power
supplies failed taking out heat would be done by certain passive means, which we had in
corporated in all our reactors. The second thing was that stress test undertaken to check the
capacity of our reactors to withstand natural calamities like earthquake etc., showed that for all
our reactors the margin for each equipment and each building was 3 to 4.5 times more. Briefly
to say that whatever intensity of earthquake was known to the area in which the reactor was
located even if 3 times more than that level occurred our nuclear reactor was safe.
16. Asked about the uranium reserves in the country, the Secretary informed that the total
reserve of uranium that we had could not support more than 15000  MW capacity and, therefore,
we had to import uranium from outside. He further added that the import of uranium would not
be perennial and after next 30 to 40 years, our Plutonium and Thorium reserves would be adequate.
17. Replying to the question of reduction in budgetary allocations as compared to the last year,
the Secretary informed that they required lesser allocation for many of the new Projects in the first
year of the XII Plan period. The Committee further wanted to know in what manner water
purification system developed in Bhabha Atomic Research Centre was different from the systems
developed by other scientific Departments like DSIR and Earth Sciences and whether the
Department had any coordination with them. Secretary replied that Department of Atomic Energy
had been doing water purification through multi stage flash evaporation process while in the DSIR,
it was mostly by the membrane process. Department of Atomic Energy too had a membrane
process and it had been doing membrane development by itself.
