PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science
and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present
the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Twenty Fifth Report of the Committee. This
Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2012-2013) of the Department of Space
(Demand No. 90).
2. In its meeting of the Committee held on the 11
th April, 2012 the Secretary and other
Officers of the Department of Space gave an overview of the various activities of the Department
and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department
to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the
clarifications sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 16
th May, 2012.
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
May 16, 2012 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.

1
REPORT
India has made an impressive array of achievements in the scientific and technological fields
since Independence. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the arena of Space. Since its inception,
the Indian Space programme, has been characterised by a vision to use space technology for the
socio-economic benefit of our people through establishment of operational space services in a self-
reliant manner. Over the last three decades, India has achieved notable progress in the design,
development and operation of space systems, as well as, using them for vital services like
telecommunication, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster warning and natural resources
survey and management. The space programme has become largely self-reliant with capability to
design and build satellites for providing space services and to launch them using indigenously
designed and developed launch vehicles. India has effectively developed space technology, applied
it successfully for its rapid developments and is presently offering a variety of space services
globally. The Space Technology has allowed the nation to move into the world of high technology,
a place previously occupied only by a few advanced nations.
2. The Indian space efforts started in the sixties with the establishment of Thumba Equatorial
Rocket Launching Station near Thiruvananthapuram. The Indian Space Research Organisation
(ISRO) was later formed in 1969. Space research activities got an additional fillip with the
formation of the Space Commission and the Department of Space in 1972. In the seventies, satellite
programmes like Aryabhatta, Bhaskara, Rohini and APPLE were conducted. The success of those
programmes led to an era of operational satellite programmes which further led to more advanced
satellites such as the INSAT and IRS series. India has since come a long way in developing a multi-
faceted and multi-dimensional space programme which is indigenous, self-reliant and applications
driven. India is now capable of building its own state of the art satellites such as the Polar Satellite
Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) series of satellites.
3. OBJECTIVES OF INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME
3.1 The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the development and
application of space technology and space science for the socio-economic benefit of the nation
through establishment of operational space services in a self-reliant manner. The main thrust areas
of the programme are:
■ Satellite-based communication and navigation for various applications.
■ Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring.
■ Meteorological applications.
■ Space Science Research and Planetary Exploration.
■ Development and operationalisation of indigenously built satellites, launch vehicles and
associated ground segment for providing these space-based services.
4. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP
4.1 The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the
Space Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)
and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric
Research Laboratory (NARL), North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), Semi-conductor
Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST).

2
4.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in
Bengaluru. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall programmes like
satellite communication, satellite navigation, earth observation, launch vehicle, space science,
atmospheric science, space industry development, disaster management support, international co-
operation, publications and public relations, budget and economic analysis and human resource
development.
4.3 The major Centres, Units and establishments of DOS/ISRO, responsible for carrying out
research and development activities as well as for undertaking various projects and programmes,
are given below:
(a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology
base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development;
(b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities at Bengaluru,
Thiruvananthapuram and Mahendragiri, is responsible for development of liquid
propulsion and cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite launch vehicles;
(c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the
launch base and also provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors;
(d) ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bengaluru, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for
the satellite development;
(e) Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bengaluru has the responsibility for
development and production of electro optical sensors for satellites;
(f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, carries out research and development in
space applications as well as development of application payloads;
(g) Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad, is involved in
the conception, definition, planning and socio/techno-economic evaluation of
developmental space applications;
(h) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision
support for disaster management;
(i) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun is a premier training and
educational institute set up for developing trained professionals in the field of Remote
Sensing, Geoinformatics and GPS Technology for Natural Resources, Environmental
and Disaster Management;
(j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground stations
at Bengaluru, Sriharikota, Lucknow, Bearslake (USA), Biak (Indonesia), Brunei and
Mauritius provides the telemetry, tracking and command support and spacecraft
mission management for the Indian remote sensing satellite missions, space science
missions and satellite launch vehicle programmes;
(k) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan, Karnataka and backup
facility at Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh have the responsibility for control and operation of
INSAT/GSAT/METSAT satellites; and
(l) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, carries out research and
development in the area of inertial systems for satellites and launch vehicles.

3
4.4 A National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), with the Department of
Space (DOS) as the nodal agency, has been established to ensure optimal utilisation of natural
resources using remote sensing data in conjunction with conventional techniques. Under NNRMS,
five Regional Remote Sensing Service Centres (RRSSCs) at Bengaluru, Dehradun, Jodhpur,
Kharagpur and Nagpur have been set up  for execution of remote sensing application programmes
in the respective regions. With effect from December, 2009, the RRSSCs have been redesignated
as Regional Remote Sensing Centres (RRSCs); while RRSC, Dehradun has been merged with IIRS.
4.5 The Department of Space, also have the following organisations, which receive Grants-in-
aid from the Department:
(a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported
mainly by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences.
(b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near
Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research.
(c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an autonomous
body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs for
developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region.
(d) The Semi-conductor Laboratory located at Chandigarh is a research and development
society and is entrusted with the design and development of Very Large Scale
Integrated Circuit (VLSI) devices and development of micro-electronic systems to meet
the strategic needs of the country.
(e) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body
under the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to
suit the requirements of state-of-art space research programme. The Institute offers
graduate, post-graduate and doctoral programmes in the area of space science,
technology and applications. Initially, IIST started the courses from the academic year
2007-08 around the existing infrastructure at Thiruvananthapuram.
4.6 Besides this, the RESPOND programme of ISRO supports sponsored research activity in
space science, space applications and space technology in various national academic/research
institutions and Space Technology Cells in premier technological institutes of the country through
grants-in-aid.
4.7 The detailed budget allocation of the Department of Space for the year 2012-13 was
considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
Environment & Forests in its meeting held on the 11
th April, 2012.
5. MONITORING MECHANISMS FOR  ONGOING SCHEMES
5.1 The Committee was informed that in order to monitor and review the progress of all the
ongoing projects/schemes and to provide overall directions, the Department has evolved a two-tier
project management structure consisting of Project/Programme Management Council and Project
Management Board/Project Executive Committee for all the major projects/schemes in the area of
Satellites, Launch Vehicles and Space applications. Multi-level reviews are carried out at the ISRO
Centres/Units and Project Management Boards/Management Councils of all the major projects/
schemes comprehensively covering the technical, managerial, cost and schedule aspects. The ISRO
Council undertakes a rigorous review of all the activities related to Projects/Schemes/Centre,
addressing the managerial/programmatic/financial aspects during the detailed technical presentations.
Further, Space Commission, during every meeting, reviews the progress of all the ongoing projects/
programmes.

4
5.2 The Department further informed that from the financial year 2011-12 onwards, it is
preparing a Results Framework Document (RFD) as part of the Performance Monitoring and
Evaluation System (PMES) for Government Departments to ensure result-oriented governance. As
a part of implementation of the RFD, the Department has clearly spelt out the Vision, Mission,
Objectives and functions of the Department, actions proposed to achieve these objectives, success
indicators to monitor and evaluate the progress in achieving policy, programme, scheme and
project. The targets set in RFD are being monitored periodically by a dedicated group to ensure
that programme targets, as set in the RFD, are met.
5.3 The Committee is of the view that an effective monitoring mechanism is vital to
ensure that the various projects are completed as per the schedule and there is no time or
cost overruns. In this context, the Committee appreciates the adoption of the Result
Framework Document (RFD) by the Department, which aims towards an effective appraisal
of the actual physical and financial progress/achievements in implementation of policies/
programs in comparison to the projected targets for each programme. The Committee, in
view of strengthening of monitoring mechanism, hopes that the Department would, in
future, be able to ensure timely completion of projects and optimum utilization of funds.
6. ELEVENTH PLAN ACHIEVEMENTS AND TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
6.1 Informing the Committee of the achievements of the Eleventh Five Year Plan, the Department
stated that the successful launch of Chandrayaan-l and the discovery of water molecules on the lunar
surface based on Chandrayaan-l scientific data, has been a landmark achievement. The Department
also informed that several of the targets set for Eleventh Five Year Plan in the area of Launch Vehicle
Development, Earth Observation Systems, Satellite Communication and Space Science research have
been achieved. In respect of some of other missions such as Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT-1),
Advanced Meteorological Satellite INSAT-3D, Multi-wavelength X-ray astronomy satellites
ASTROSAT, SARAL, GSAT-9, GSAT-10, GSAT-6/6A, GSAT-11 and IRNSS, major progress has been
achieved in Eleventh Plan although the launch of these missions would marginally spill over to the
first half of Twelfth Plan period due to technological developmental complexities, difficulties in
sourcing the critical supplies and mission contingencies.
6.2 The Committee appreciates the achievements made by the Department during the
Eleventh Plan, notably the Chandrayaan-l Mission and progress made in the field of Launch
Vehicle Development, Earth Observation and Satellite Communication Systems. However, it
notes with concern that some of the missions such as Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT-1),
Advanced Meteorological satellite INSAT-3D, Multi-wavelength X-ray astronomy satellites
ASTROSAT, SARAL, GSAT-9, GSAT-IO, GSAT-6/6A, GSAT-11 and IRNSS could not be
completed as per schedule and shall spill over to the Twelfth Plan period due to
technological developmental complexities, difficulties in sourcing the critical supplies and
mission contingencies. The Committee hopes Department would make all possible efforts to
tide over these difficulties and projects would be completed as per the revised schedule.
6.3 As regards the Twelfth Plan, the Committee was informed that an allocation of Rs. 55,000
crores was sought by the Department, consisting of Plan component of Rs. 47,500 crores and
non-Plan component of Rs. 7,500 crores.
6.4 The new programmes envisaged during Twelfth Plan includes Mars Orbiter Mission,
Advanced Cartographic Satellite-Cartosat-3, Oceansat-3, Resourcesat-3, Scatsat-l, Development of
High-throughput Communication Satellites, Human Space Flight initiatives, Multi-Object Tracking
Radar, Third Launch Pad facilities at Sriharikota, etc. The major thrust of the Indian Space
programme in the Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012-17) will be to strengthen and expand the
operational services in satellite communications and navigation, develop enhanced imaging capability

5
for natural resources management, weather, and climate change studies, undertake space science
and planetary exploratory missions for better understanding of the solar system and the universe
and to develop a heavy lift launcher. Amongst others, the Mars Orbitor Mission, Operation of GSLV
with indigenous cryogenic stage, completing the development flights of next generation GSLV
Mk III, building up the constellation of Indian Regional Navigational Satellite System and
augmenting the INSAT/GSAT system capacity to meet the pressing demand are amongst the priority
programmes envisaged for Twelfth Plan.
6.5 The Committee notes that in the Twelfth Five year Plan (2012-17) the major thrust
of the Indian Space programme will be to carry forward and strengthen the already
established space-based services aimed at socio-economic development of the country. The
Committee hopes that, apart from the ongoing space programmes and its efforts for
developing advanced launch vehicles, the Department should also strive for mastering
critical technologies, so as to reduce the chances of failure of important missions. The
Committee is of the opinion that the next stepping stone of the Department should be to
strive towards sending a Manned Mission to Space, which naturally follows from its
successes obtained in sending launch vehicles which can carry higher payloads to space.
6.6 The Committee also recommends that Department should also strive to increase its
global market share in space services by developing more innovative and competitive space
services on commercial lines and the revenue generated from marketing of these services
should be used for further growth and development of space technology in the country. This
will also increasingly reduce the dependence of our space programme on budgetary resources.

demonstrate the capability to carry human beings to low earth orbit and their safe return back to
earth. The mission was initiated in the year 2006 and the scheduled launch is likely to take place

Department stated as Phase-I of the Programme pertaining to design, development, and flight
testing of crew module, PS4 augmented service module and development of crew escape system
was not approved, the allocation for R.E. 2010-11 was reduced limiting the expenditure only to pre-
project phase. However, the allocation for B.E. 2012-13 was increased to Rs. 60.46 crores, to

research and technological support for timely execution of the project. The Committee,

9. CHANDRAYAAN-2 AND MARS ORBITOR MISSION
9.1 The Committee was informed that Chandrayaan-2 is a follow-on mission to send an orbiter
and lander rover to moon by 2014-15, with an objective of expanding the scientific knowledge
about the moon, over and above what has been learnt about this natural earth satellite, through
Chandrayaan-1 mission. The Committee has been further given to understand that Government has
approved the undertaking of Chandrayaan-2 mission in September, 2008. The total estimated cost
of Chandrayaan-2 is Rs. 425.00 crores. The work on realisation of payloads and spacecraft
sub-systems is in progress.
9.2 The Mars Orbiter Mission, envisages launching a space craft to reach and orbit around
Mars, using a PSLV launch vehicle during November, 2013. In this connection a study report on
the feasibility of undertaking a planned Mission to Mars has been completed and it has been found
feasible to undertake India’s first mission to Mars during the early phase of Twelfth Plan.
9.3 The Committee while interacting with the Department of Space on 11
th April, 2012, raised
a query regarding the constant rescheduling of Chandrayaan-2 programme, initially from 2010 to
2011 and then to January, 2012. In response to the query the Department stated that Chandrayaan-
2 involves a complex work of sending a lander and a robot to moon for doing experiment on this
satellite. The Department further stated that the lander is made by Russia while the rover is made
in India. While narrating further on the issue, the Department pointed out, that due to
reprioritisation of certain programme by Russia, the Chandrayaan-2 programme has been postponed
to 2014. Moreover, recent three failures in GSLV flights, has placed the Department in a
disadvantageous position to prove the reliability of GSLV mission, which is now taking time.
9.4 Similarly, in case of Mars Mission which is more of a complex mission than Chandrayaan-
2, involving 300 days movement of satellite to Mars through a complex propulsion system that
should sustain for 300 days. Accordingly, the initial plan is to send an orbiter to Mars in 2013,
and if it fails, the projected date will be shifted to 2016 or to 2018 as the time when such a
Mission can be sent is dictated by the geometry of Mars-Earth-Sun.
9.5 The Committee after going thoroughly through the aforesaid reply of the
Department is of the opinion that preparation of an optimistic schedule for missions like
Chandrayaan-2 and Mars Orbitor Mission, alone is not sufficient but what is required is the
will and dedication to complete the mission target within the time schedule. If time
schedule does not inspire the confidence of the team and is seen by it as an unrealistic
target, it will hardly serve any purpose. The Department should, therefore, fix time
schedules in a more realistic way, rather than fixing time schedules which are not to be
adhered. The Committee feels that failure to adhere to programme schedule sends a wrong
message to the public and lowers their confidence in our capability to take our space
programme to new heights. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
schedule for all missions including complex missions should be prepared only after taking
into account all ground realities, so that a realistic schedule meant to be adhered by all,
rather than that being violated with impunity, is prepared.

comprehensive analysis of the actual fund requirement for the programme. Scarce

plan its projects efficiently, set realistic targets and its determination to achieve the targets

12. TELEMEDICINE
12.1 The Committee was also informed of one of the unique applications of Space Technology
for societal benefit is in the field of healthcare. The programme, Telemedicine, which started in
2001 has been connecting remote/rural/medical college hospitals and Mobile Units through the
Indian Satellites to major speciality hospitals in cities and towns. Presently, the network covers the
areas of Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Andaman & Lakshdweep Islands, North Eastern States and
other mainland States including tribal districts of States like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu,
Chhattisgarh, Punjab, West Bengal, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Rajasthan.
The ISRO telemedicine network covers about 382 hospitals with 306 remote/rural/district/medical
college hospitals and 16 Mobile Telemedicine units being connected to 60 speciality hospitals. The
Mobile Telemedicine units cover diverse areas of Opthalmology, Cardiology, Radiology, Diabetology,
Mammography, general medicine, women and child health.
12.2 The Committee was informed that the Department of Space provides Telemedicine systems
software, hardware and communication equipment, as well as satellite bandwidth, while State
Governments and the speciality hospitals give funds for the infrastructure, manpower and facility
support.
12.3 On being enquired about the steps have been initiated by the Department to expand Tele-
medicine network to the far-flung regions in the country, the Department informed that the band
width required for expansion of Telemedicine network was earlier planned onboard GSAT-5P
satellite with 12 Extended C band transponders. However, due to the failure of the launch vehicle
carrying the GSAT-5P satellite, the expansion of Telemedicine network could not be realised as
planned due to satellite bandwidth limitations. However, with the successful launch of GSAT-12 on
July 15, 2011 onboard India’s PSLY , the required transponder capacity to support Telemedicine
activities has been restored. Currently, the migration of existing Tele-medicine network to the new
GSAT-12 satellite is in progress and after operationalising the existing Telemedicine nodes with
GSAT-12 satellite, the expansion of Telemedicine facility will be pursued.
12.4 The Committee feels that Telemedicine is a very useful programme pursued by the
Department for providing societal benefits by use of space technology to the common
masses. The Committee is aware that to provide even the basic healthcare facilities in all
the villages of the country, would require a huge capital investment, both in terms of
manpower and resources. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that this is a very
cost-effective method for providing quality health care facilities in the rural and remote

10
areas of the country. The Committee recommends that the telemedicine network should be
expanded in a time bound manner to cover the backward, remote, inaccessible or disease-
prone areas, left out so far.
12.5 The Committee also notes that due to the failure of the launch vehicle carrying the
GSAT-5P satellite, the expansion of telemedicine network work was adversely affected. The
Committee is happy to note that with the successful launch of GSAT-12, the telemedicine
activities are being restored. The Committee hopes that the migration of telemedicine
network to GSAT-12 satellite, which is currently in progress, will be completed soon and the

13. DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT SYSTEM
13.1 The Committee has been informed that the Disaster Management Support (DMS)
Programme of ISRO provides continued support towards disaster management in the country
through products and services emanating from the space and airborne systems, both imaging and
communications. The DMS-Decision Support Centre (DMS-DSC) established at National Remote

drought, landslides, earthquakes and forest fires. The information generated from aero-space

providing emergency communication for disaster management activities, and at the behest of
Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), ISRO has set up a satellite based Virtual Private Network (VPN)
linking the National Control Room at MHA with DMS-DSC at NRSC, important national agencies,
key Government Offices in Delhi and the Control Rooms of 22 multi-hazard-prone States.
13.2 When the Committee enquired the Department about the utilization of ‘Virtual Private
Network (VPN)’ for networking the State and District level emergency control centres during
natural disasters and the achievements of the Department in this regard, specially during the recent
natural disasters, the Department informed that in 2011-12, the Virtual Private Network was utilised
by Decision Support Centre, NRSC (National Remote Sensing Centre) for dissemination of value
added products to the States such as Orissa, Assam and Bihar. A primary node has been added
during 2011 at North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NESAC), Shillong, making the total
number of nodes to 35. The network is being re-activated with a full transponder on-board GSAT-
12 and it is expected that the network will be fully ready for utilisation by end of April, 2012.
13.3 The Committee is of the view that natural disasters such as floods, droughts,
cyclones, earthquakes and landslides are a recurring phenomena and every year widespread
economic devastation and loss of human lives is caused on account of these natural
calamities. The Committee is of the opinion that the services of Virtual Private Network
(VPN) which has been set up for networking the State and district level emergency control
centres for natural disasters management must be optimally utilized for rapid dissemination
of information to lessen the human and economic loss.

15. FAILURE ANALYSIS COMMITTEE (FAC)
15.1 In response to a query raised by the Committee regarding the appointment of Failure
Analysis Committee to go into the causes of failure of two GSLV flights into space during 2010,
the Department has stated that during the last financial year GSLV-D3, carrying the GSAT-4
spacecraft was unsuccessful on April 15, 2010 and again the launch of GSLV-F06 carrying GSAT-
5P spacecraft failed on December 25, 2010. The Failure Analysis Committee concluded that in case
of GSLV-D3, the anomalous stoppage of the fuel booster turbo pump of the indigenous cryogenic
stage shortly after the ignition of the cryogenic engine was the cause for the mission failure.
Regarding the GSLV-F06, Failure Analysis Committee concluded that the primary cause of the
failure is the untimely and inadvertent snapping of a group of ten connectors located at the bottom
portion of the Russian Cryogenic Stage. The Department has further stated that based on the
recommendations of the Failure Analysis Committees, the Fuel Booster Turbo Pump and the Lower
Shroud of the Indigenous Cryogenic Stage has been redesigned and qualification test are in progress.
15.2 While deliberating on the issue on 11th April, 2012, the Chairman of the Committee queried
about the updating of the aerodynamic characteristics of GSLV configuration which has been made
as per the Failure Analysis Committee recommendations. The Department while responding to the
query mentioned that due to high aerodynamic load, the GSLV F06 failed, as the mass of the
satellite was increased from 1800kg to 2200kg leading to significant increase in the payload and
also increase in diameter of the heat shield to 4 metre.
15.3 In reply to another query, the Department also opined that in future all GSLV vehicles and
other advanced launch vehicles, should be powered with indigenous cryogenic stage as doubts have
been raised about the efficiency of Russian cryogenic technology after the failure of GSLV series
of satellites.
15.4 After going through the replies of the Department of Space and findings of FAC, the
Committee is of the opinion that the Department should make efforts to develop our

12
indigenous cryogenic engines for GSLV and other advanced launch vehicles, as it would
make us self-reliant in this important area. The Committee would, however like the
Department to ensure that every possible care is taken while launching our satellite so that
chances of failure are reduced to the minimum. It should bear in mind that any failure of
our missions, though failures are bound to happen in such complex missions, not only
results in loss of crores of rupees but also raises a doubt in the mind of the people about
the credibility of our space programme.
16. The Committee after examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants

competence that the Department has exhibited and the kind of core and critical
programmes that they have envisaged for future, the Committee strongly recommends that
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance should provide adequate funds for
completion of projects and schemes undertaken by the Department.

programmes, there has been a trend to seek substantial budgetary allocations at B.E. stage
without making an extensive and critical assessment of the actual requirements. The
Committee feels that budgetary demands should be sought by the Department only after
comprehensive analysis of the actual fund requirement for the programme. Scarce
resources should not be blocked by asking for ambitious allocations and not utilizing them
subsequently. These instances are also a reflection on the capacity of the Department to
plan its projects efficiently, set realistic targets and its determination to achieve the targets
set. (Para 11.5)
10. The Committee feels that Telemedicine is a very useful programme pursued by the
Department for providing societal benefits by use of space technology to the common
masses.  The Committee is aware that to provide even the basic healthcare facilities in all
the villages of the country, would require a huge capital investment, both in terms of
manpower and resources. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that this is a very
cost effective method for providing quality health care facilities in the rural and remote

15
areas of the country. The Committee recommends that the telemedicine network should be
expanded in a time bound manner to cover the backward, remote, inaccessible or disease-
prone areas, left out so far. (Para 12.4)
11. The Committee also notes that due to the failure of the launch vehicle carrying the
GSAT-5P satellite, the expansion of telemedicine network work was adversely affected. The
Committee is happy to note that with the successful launch of GSAT-12, the telemedicine
activities are being restored. The Committee hopes that the migration of telemedicine
network to GSAT-12 satellite, which is currently in progress, will be completed soon and the
expansion of the facility will be pursued with vigour. (Para 12.5)
12. The Committee is of the view that natural disasters such as floods, droughts,
cyclones, earthquakes and landslides are a recurring phenomena and every year widespread
economic devastation and loss of human lives is caused on account of these natural
calamities. The Committee is of the opinion that the services of Virtual Private Network
(VPN) which has been set up for networking the State and district level emergency control
centres for natural disasters management must be optimally utilized for rapid dissemination
of information to lessen the human and economic loss. (Para 13.3)
13. The Committee is of the opinion that active involvement and effective participation
of more and more Indian industries in providing quality products and services needed for
our Space programme will lead to self-reliance and would decrease our dependence on
foreign industries for space equipments and technologies. The involvement of Indian
industries in production of aggregates/systems for the Indian Space programme would
augment the technical expertise of the Indian industry and would also lead to employment
generation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Space should
make concerted efforts in this direction. The Committee also desires that Department of
Space should look forward to transfer more and more technologies which may be useful for
civilian applications to Indian Industries so as to make them globally competitive.
(Para 14.3)
14. After going through the replies of the Department of Space and findings of FAC, the
Committee is of the opinion that the Department should make efforts to develop our
indigenous cryogenic engines for GSLV and other advanced launch vehicles, as it would
make us self-reliant in this important area. The Committee would, however, like the
Department to ensure that every possible care is taken while launching our satellite so that
chances of failure are reduced to the minimum. It should bear in mind that any failure of
our missions, though failures are bound to happen in such complex  missions, not only
results in loss of crores of rupees but also raises a doubt in the mind of the people about
the credibility of our space programme. (Para 15.4)
15. The Committee after examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants
(2012-13) of the Department of Space, is of the view that the Department, through its
various schemes and programmes, is realising the immense potential of space technology
for national development and in solving the problems of common man. Keeping in view the
excellent and outstanding work that the Department of Space has undertaken, the kind of
competence that the Department has exhibited and the kind of core and critical
programmes that they have envisaged for future, the Committee strongly recommends that
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance should provide adequate funds for
completion of projects and schemes undertaken by the Department. (Para 16)

and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present
the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Twenty Sixth Report of the Committee. This
Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2012- 2013) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences
(Demand No. 29).
2. In its meeting of the Committee held on the 13
th April, 2012 the Secretary and other
Officers of the Ministry of Earth Sciences gave an overview of the various activities of the
Ministry and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the
Ministry to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the
clarifications sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 16

DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,

Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.

1
REPORT
Since the time immemorial, Oceans have always fascinated man and influenced his life and
history in several ways. Even today, man obtains mineral, food and energy resources from the
oceans. Due to its vastness and interplay of ecological processes, oceans control the atmosphere
and global climate besides being a vast storehouse of resources necessary for sustenance of life
on earth. The magnitude of India’s vast ocean resources can be considered from the fact that the
coastline of the mainland and islands measures about 7,500 kms. and the area of Exclusive
Economic Zone (EEZ) of the country is 2.02 million sq. km. The coastal and offshore environment
support a wide variety of marine ecosystem, rich in species and diversity, besides supporting
multifarious economic development activities. The sea has tremendous influence on the physical and
meteorological conditions of the country.
2. In view of great importance and significance of the subject, Government of India
established the Department of Ocean Development in 1981 (later renamed as Ministry of Earth
Sciences) with an aim to create a deeper understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and
central Indian Ocean and also to develop technology and technological aids for harnessing of
marine resources in a sustainable way and for holistic understanding of the earth processes in order
to achieve greater accuracy in the forecast of weather, climate and hazards.
3. The Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) has created an executive arm for its policies and
programmes, namely ‘The Earth System Science Organisation (ESSO)’, in the year October, 2007,
subsequent to the setting up of the MoES, which was formed in 2006 by bringing all the agencies
of meteorological and ocean development activities under one umbrella, recognizing the importance
of strong coupling among various components of the earth, viz. atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere
and geosphere. The Ministry inter alia  is primarily responsible for development of technology
towards the exploration and exploitation of marine resources in a sustainable way for the socio-
economic benefit of the society by taking into account the global developments in the field of
marine environment and to provide a wide range of meteorological services to the Indian public in
general and to the various sectors specifically. The area of competence of the Ministry, covers a
gamut of policies and programmes that relate to the areas of Weather viz. Weather advisories
specific to agriculture, aviation, shipping, sports, monsoon, disasters (cyclone, earthquake, tsunami,
sea level rise), living (fishery advisory) and non-living resources (poly-metallic nodules, gas
hydrates, freshwater); Coastal and Marine Ecosystems and Climate Change.
4. OBJECTIVES AND FUNCTIONS OF THE MINISTRY
The Ministry of Earth Sciences has the following objectives and functions:
• Improving weather forecast and provide advisory to agriculture, aviation, shipping,
sports including the Extended Long Range Seasonal Monsoon forecast;
• Providing a wide range of ocean information advisories including fishery information;
• Improving the understanding of Polar Science and its implications for climate change;
• Developing technology for harnessing marine resources;
• Conducting survey for assessing non-living resources;
• Assesing coastal marine productivity and Marine Ecosystems;
• Improving understanding of Climate Change Science;

2
•  Providing early warning of natural hazards viz. cyclone, tsunami, sea level rise; and
•  Promoting basic research including capacity building in the Earth System Science.
5. ORGANISATIONAL SET UP
5.1 The Ministry of Earth Sciences functions through the Earth Commission. The executive arm
of the Ministry i.e.  ‘The Earth System Science Organisation (ESSO)’ is responsible for
implementing its policies and programmes. It has four major branches of earth sciences viz.,
(i) Ocean Science and Technology Services; (ii) Atmospheric and Climate Science Services;
(iii) Geoscience and Technology; and (iv) Polar Science and Cryosphere. The policies/programmes
of the ESSO are being pursued through its autonomous bodies and subordinate offices. The
institutions, under the ESSO includes, India Meteorological Department (IMD), National Centre for
Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) and Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology
(IITM), National Centre for Antarctica and Ocean Research (NCAOR), National Institute of Ocean
Technology (NIOT), Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Centre for
Marine Living Resources (CMLRE) and Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM).
5.2 Operationalisation of Earth Commission:
The Committee was also informed that the Earth Commission was constituted by Hon’ble
Prime Minister after Cabinet approval, on the pattern of Space Commission and Atomic Energy
Commission. The Earth System Science Organisation with a Council to formulate policies has also
been constituted under the Earth Commission by the Minister of Earth Sciences. However, the
Earth Commission presently does not have any financial and administrative powers.
5.3 The Committee feels that without any financial and administrative powers, the Earth
Commission will hardly be effective in performing its role and functions and the very
purpose of setting up of Earth Commission would be defeated. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that immediate steps be taken to provide necessary financial and
administrative powers to the Earth Commission so that it may carry out it assigned role
effectively.
5.4 The detailed budget allocation of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, for the year 2012-2013
was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests in a meeting held on 13th April, 2012.
6. MONITORING AND REVIEWING ONGOING SCHEMES
6.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that a 3-tier mechanism has been adopted by the
Ministry to monitor and review various schemes. While at the programme level, the schemes are
monitored by Steering Committee constituted by the Ministry with experts drawn from relevant
fields, at institute level, particularly for the autonomous bodies, the programmes are monitored
periodically by the, Governing Council, Financial Committee and Research Advisory Committee of
the Centres. At the Ministry level, the programmes are monitored on half yearly basis by the ESSO
council, in the beginning of the financial year (in April) and middle of the year (in September).
Besides, the programmes are being monitored and evaluated by Planning Commission and Cabinet
Secretariat as regards the Result Framework Document (RFD) on annual and half yearly basis,
respectively.
6.2 The Committee was further informed that the Ministry is making every effort to monitor
and evaluate the progress of the programmes. All the centres of the Ministry have been connected
to Tele-presence system for periodic monitoring on both scientific and financial aspects of

3
programmes by the Secretary, MoES. The financial progress of the autonomous bodies of the
centres is also being monitored on quarterly basis by the Additional Secretary and Financial Advisor
(AS&FA) of the Mini stry using tele-presence on quarterly basis.
6.3 The Committee notes with satisfaction that Result Framework Document (RFD), has
been adopted by the Ministry to review and monitor physical and financial progress/
achievements of major activities with respect to agreed targets fixed for each programme,
in addition to its internal monitoring mechanisms. The Committee is of the opinion that an
effective monitoring mechanism is imperative for ensuring that the various projects are
completed as per the projected schedule and timely action taken to overcome problems that
may arise in the implementation of the projects. The Committee hopes that with potent
monitoring mechanisms, the Ministry would be able to complete its projects in time.
7. ELEVENTH PLAN ACHIEVEMENTS AND TWELFTH PLAN PROPOSALS
7.1 Citing the achievements during the XIth Plan period (2007-2012), the Ministry informed the
Committee that the major focus during this Plan period was on the observation systems for
improving services related to oceanic, geological and atmospheric hazards and improving short-term
forecasts. Some of the major achievements during this period, inter-alia  include setting up of the
state-of-the-art tsunami warning system, two desalination plants in the Lakshadweep Islands, Centre
for Climate Change Research, advanced training school for earth system science and climate
change, third polar station at the Larsemann Hills in Antarctica, Establishment of Arctic Station,
high performance computing facility, etc. Besides various services were augmented/improved such
as agro-meteorology for farmers, forecasting for fog, weather, air quality, monsoon and cyclone,
etc. On being enquired from the Ministry, it was also informed that all the projects launched during
XIth Plan have been successfully achieved baring two projects viz., Multi-channel Seismic System
on board Sagar Kanya and NIOT extension centre in West Bengal.
7.2 As regards the XIIth Plan, the Committee was informed that the outlay proposed for by
the Ministry was Rs.18,824 crores. The Working Group and Steering Committee, have proposed
a total of 76 projects (both new and ongoing) for implementation during the XIIth Plan. In order
to focus the activities for accomplishing the targets and meet objectives, the Ministry had
reoriented and recast the 76 projects of XIIth Plan into 15 major programmes. The focus during
the XIIth Plan would be on discovering new phenomena, exploring sea bed and Polar Regions,
understanding of various earth processes and their interaction, developing earth system science
model and application of knowledge for improving/developing services for societal benefits. Another
major task, would be to develop climate services in view of climate change and variability, besides
continuing the operational programmes related to observations of atmosphere, ocean, snow, ice and
land surface and services related to weather and hazards. The major missions planned are related
to monsoon, earthquake, mountain meteorology, cloud physics, ocean mineral exploration
particularly Hydrothermal Sulfides, acquisition of observing platforms, such as aircrafts and ships,
and augmenting observing systems and earth enterprise, monsoon mission.
7.3 In this connection the Committee would like to invite the attention of the Ministry
to its 204th Report (page 3, para 5.1) on the Demands for Grants (2010-11), wherein it has
been stated that as per information furnished by the Ministry, the total initial Budgetary
allocation of Rs. 7004.00 crores for the XIth Five Year Plan was revised to Rs. 6637.00
crores at the mid term appraisal stage. In comparison to this, the Committee has observed

10. AUTONOMOUS BODIES
I. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF  OCEAN TECHNOLOGY  (NIOT), CHENNAI
10.1 The National Institute of Ocean Technology was started in 1993 as the technical arm with
a view to develop reliable indigenous technology to solve the various engineering problems
associated with harnessing of non-living and living resources in the Indian Exclusive Economic
Zone (EEZ), which is about two-thirds of the land area of India. Its major functions are
development of technology related to the country’s needs in the field of deep sea mining,
desalination, ocean energy, marine instrumentation, materials development, oceanic data collecting
devices and observation systems etc. in consonance with ocean policy and national priorities,
Research and development of ocean related technology projects sponsored by the industry and
development of required technologies for the management of coastal zone and islands of the country.
10.2 The Committee was also informed that due to the re-orientation of the activities of the
Ministry, the allocation for NIOT, has been provided for under the ‘Ocean Technology Programme’
where a total allocation of Rs. 89.00 crores has been made.
10.3 The Ministry also informed that it has adopted the ‘Low Temperature Thermal Desalination
(LTTD)’ to solve the drinking water problem and two LTTD plants were commissioned in the
islands of Lakshadweep, one each at Minicoy and Agatti during March, 2011 and August, 2011
respectively. These plants, with a capacity of one lakh litre per day have been contributing
significantly to the drinking water needs of the local population of these islands. The Ministry
proposes to set up six more plants in other islands of Lakshadweep one each at Amini, Chetlet,
Kadamath, Kalpeni, Kiltan and Andrott, through public-private partnership mode.
10.4 The Committee has always stressed upon the need for greater application of
technologies for socio-economic development of common masses. The Committee, therefore,
commends the initiative of the NIOT in using technology i.e. ‘Low Temperature Thermal
Desalination (LTTD)’ to solve the drinking water problem in two islands of Lakshadweep,
by setting up two LTTD plants. The Committee is also happy to know that NIOT, also
proposes to set up six more plants in other islands of Lakshadweep, through public-private
partnership mode.  The Committee is of the opinion that such technologies needs to be
popularized and such plants should also be established in Andaman and Nicobar Islands as
well and other coastal regions of the country, which face a scarcity of fresh drinking water.
It also feels that the adoption of the public-private partnership model would make the
establishment of such plants more  cost effective, and enable the Ministry to commission a
larger number of plants in the coastal regions of the country in a short time.

6
II. INDIAN NATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN INFORMATION SERVICES (INCOIS),
HYDERABAD
10.5 The mission of INCOIS is to provide ocean information and advisory services to the
society, industry, government and scientific community through sustained ocean observations and
constant improvements through systematic and focused research. The objective is to provide
coastal and ocean advisory services, potential fishing zone advisory service (PFZ), ocean state
forecast, national tsunami early warning etc. The Tsunami and Storm Surge Early Warning System
started in October, 2007 at INCOIS provides information on ocean waves swell etc. which are
quite valuable for Navy, Coast Guards, Merchant Ships. Similarly Fishing Zone Advisories are
utilized by large number of fishermen.
10.6 The Committee was also informed that during the current fiscal, the INCOIS and Tsunami
and Storm Surge have been included in the programme ‘Ocean Science and Services’ for which
an allocation of Rs. 91.00 crores has been made.
10.7 The Ministry informed that performance related to cyclone warnings has been significantly
improved due to implementation of high-resolution models and augmentation of capability to acquire
atmospheric and ocean data and as a part of disaster warning services, the Coastal Vulnerability
Mapping Index (CVI) for both Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands have been
completed. The centre has been recognized as a Regional Tsunami Service Provider (RTSP) for the
Indian Ocean Region and started its operation for the Indian Ocean Rim countries. A Pan–India
mock drill exercise was successfully conducted on October 12, 2011, as part of Tsunami Warning
System in coordination with 29 countries of Indian Ocean under the overall framework of Inter-
governmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO programme and with this exercise, the
Indian Tsunami Warning System established by the Ministry at INCOIS, Hyderabad has been
entrusted responsibility for operation of Indian Tsunami Warning System as Regional Tsunami
Service Provider by UNESCO.
10.8 The Committee commends the efforts of the Ministry in augmenting the scientific
and technological capabilities of the INCOIS, in respect of predicting cyclones and tsunami,
since accurate and advance warnings about these natural hazards give sufficient time to
disaster management agencies to gear themselves better to minimise the loss of property
and lives. The Committee is also happy to note that the Indian Tsunami Warning System,
has been entrusted the responsibility to function as Regional Tsunami Service Provider by
UNESCO and have started its operation for the Indian Ocean Rim countries. The
Committee commends the Ministry for making accurate predictions on recent earthquake
that hit certain parts of India and saving the country from unnecessary anxiety and fear.
The Committee appreciates the fact that the technological capabilities of the INCOIS have
been recognized internationally and hopes that, in future, the Centre would forge
collaborations with similar scientific organizations of the advanced countries, to provide
ocean information and advisory services to society, industry, Government agencies and
scientific community through sustained ocean observations, information management, and
focused research.

10.9 The mission of NCAOR is to plan, promote, co-ordinate and execute the entire gamut of
polar science and logistic activities of the country in order to ensure a perceptible presence of India
in Antarctica and Arctic and to uphold our strategic interests in the global framework of nations

11. CLOUD SEEDING PROGRAMME
11.1 During its deliberations with the Ministry on the 13
th April, 2012, a query was raised by the
Committee regarding differences of opinion among scientists on the cloud seeding programme in
different States. Citing a particular case, it was pointed that the programme under Andhra Pradesh
Government had resulted in improved rainfall, while in case of Karnataka Government no such
improvement in rainfall was observed. The Ministry apprised the Committee that doing cloud
seeding randomly on any cloud will not yeild rain and understanding the nature of the cloud is a
must before seeding. The Ministry further informed the Committee that selecting a right type of
cloud before seeding can enhance the precipitation ratio. The Ministry further pointed out that lack

8
of availability of correct data leads to the difficulty in seeding the right type of cloud for yielding
precipitation. An aircraft was hired two years back to measure cloud behaviour, but as the study
was sporadic the complete understanding of cloud physics is still to be achieved. The Ministry
further apprised that a special laboratory to study clouds has been established at Mahabaleshwar.
11.2 The Committee is of the opinion that research in the field of cloud physics should
be accorded high priority as it would not only help in right selection of clouds for seeding
but would help master its other aspects as well including development of cost effective
techniques for successful cloud seeding, which may go a long way in helping the country
solve the problems of drought and water scarcity in certain parts of the country. Such
research may also provide greater insights in understanding the dynamics of global
warming. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that Ministry should make all
out efforts to strengthen the special laboratory which has been set up at Mahabaleshwar to
study all kinds of clouds from precipitation point of view so that cost effective techniques
for artificial precipitation could be developed and for that, if needed, adequate funds should
be made available.
12. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMMES
12.1 The Research and Development activities of the Ministry cover experimental work and
research on basic and applied meteorology and seismology including design and development of the
instruments for it. The Ministry also informed that one of the significant achievements under the
programme has been the improvement in the long range forecast of Indian summer monsoon. The
Ministry also informed the Committee of the following achievements, in the Research and
Development, made by it.
(i) Improvement in weather forecasting:  Research and Development efforts are driven by
operational requirements to improve the multi-scale weather forecasts and need based R & D
efforts have been developed to translate research to operation. Specific efforts have been made
towards the assimilation of Doppler Weather Observations for forecasting and meso-scale modeling,
application of multi-model ensemble (MME) technique for weather forecasting the district level
rainfall, cyclones etc. and about 12 papers in national as well as international journals have
published in this regard.
(ii) Improvement in application of weather forecast in agriculture : In order to improve the
operational Agromet Services, research work is being carried out in different areas like development
of forewarning models for pest and disease incidences, delineation of agroclimatic zones under the
present scenario of rainfall and irrigation, resilience of climate change and its impact on agromet
services including field experiments on rate of photosynthesis at different environmental conditions
and other different areas of agrometeorology. The salient findings emerging from these studies are
being experimentally used in Operational Agromet Services.
(iii) Improvement in Meteorological Instruments:  A new hall effect Wind direction sensor has
been developed by the IMD, which is capable of showing wind direction even at very low wind
speed. A PC based Current Weather instrument system, with very high resolution has been designed
and installed at IGI airport. A Lightning protection system has been designed for protection against
lightning and surges and installed at Cochin, Calicut, Thiruvananthapuram Airports. A new technique
has been developed, which has helped IMD to get real time radiation data from network stations
on IMD website, at ten minutes interval which can be accessed at any location.
(iv) Rainfall Analysis for drought monitoring :  To monitor droughts, research have been
made towards studying the trend in extreme rainfall and district-wise droughts and results were
brought out in a peer reviewed research journal.

9
(v) Climatic Monitoring:  Reports on Climate Monitoring are regularly brought out in national
and international journals for the benefit of the scientific community.

12.3 The Committee is happy to note that allocations made for R&D activities of IMD and
for the programmes ‘Research, Training, Education and Outreach’ taken together are

13. NATIONAL CENTRE OF SEISMOLOGY (NCS)
13.1 The Committee during its deliberations with the Ministry, on the 13th April, 2012, enquired
about the existence of a separate research institute to study the science behind earthquakes. The
Ministry in response to the said query mentioned that it has already proposed to set up a separate
body in this regard, under the nomenclature ‘National Centre of Seismology’.
13.2 The Ministry further mentioned that the issue of setting up a separate Institute/Centre for
Seismology has been under consideration since 1969. Various committees viz., Bhagwantam
Committee have recommended viz., Narasimha Committee (2007) and Das Committee (2007), have
recommended separate Centre for Seismology. Presently, it is proposed to have a separate
Seismology Division for IMD. The newly set up Earthquake Risk Evaluation Centre (EREC) will
be consolidated into a separate ‘National Centre for Seismology’ (NCS), to enable rapid scientific
developments in this field.
13.3 The Ministry further informed that, at present, various aspects of seismology related
research are being carried out in a fragmented way by several research, academic and State and
Central Government institutions in the country. India Meteorological Department, under the Ministry
of Earth Sciences (MoES), has been the nodal agency of Government of India dealing with matters
related to Seismology in the country. The Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) is currently
supporting several multi-institutional R&D projects in Seismology. The Ministry therefore stated
that, there is an urgent need to bring synergy that would effectively integrate in a holistic manner
all the efforts put in by various Earth Science related organizations in the country, by way of
creating a centre of excellence in Seismology, called the NCS, that would address all earthquake
related matters.
13.4 The Ministry further mentioned that the ultimate aim of the NCS would be to enhance our
understanding of earthquake processes, especially those relevant to India, and provide S&T inputs
on the earthquake hazard for populated areas, thereby reducing the risk due to earthquakes. In
terms of economic implications, the benefits that would be accrued in terms of reducing the loss

10
of life and damage to property in future from earthquakes, would be much more than the
investments made.
13.5 The Committee fully understands that though it may not humanly possible to
completely control the forces of nature like earthquake, yet through technological
interventions the massive destruction and financial losses it causes can certainly be
minimized. The Committee, therefore, feels that, intensive efforts towards scientific
research are needed to fully understand the various aspects of earthquakes. It is therefore,
imperative to establish a separate institutional mechanism to effectively deal with
earthquake related issues in the country, so as to minimize the damage in future due to
earthquakes.
13.6 The Committee also notes that  p resently, various aspects of seismology related
research are being carried out in a fragmented way by several research, academic and State
and Central Government institutions in the country.  In view of the extreme killer and
destructive potential of earthquake as a natural phenomenon, the Committee fully endorses
the proposal of the Ministry to set up a separate research institute of the nature of
‘National Centre of Seismology’ which is exclusively devoted to study of the mechanics of
earthquakes, geo-tectonic movements and all other aspects of earthquake so as to avoid/
minimise the loses of life and property, a field which is yet to by mastered by the human
mind.

16. ACCURACY IN WEATHER FORECASTING
16.1 The Committee notes that during discussions on the application of Numerical weather
modelling for the purpose of weather forecast, with the Ministry on the 13
th April, 2012, it was
informed by the Ministry that USA is more advanced as regards meteorological predications than
India, because it uses high speed computing system than India to frame weather models and they
also have sufficiently trained a large number of people to run and understand those models which
India lacks. Therefore the Ministry proposes to enhance India’s computing power in the field of
meteorology by establishing schools to train people so that the country can attain the US level
efficiency in the next five years. While explaining the efficiency of Numerical Weather Modelling,
the Ministry stated that it represents atmospheric conditions, through a set of equations solved
through high performance computers, through which the prediction period in advance could be
reduced from five days at present to two days. He further apprised the Committee that Numerical
Modelling is very important to generate initial weather conditions based upon which future
predictions are made.
16.2 In response to another query regarding level of accuracy in forecasting raised by the
Committee, the Ministry replied that Numerical Weather prediction will bring India at par with US
Centres in terms of accuracy in prediction, in the next five years and forecast improvement will
take place in terms of accuracy upto five days.
16.3 The Committee feels that the above discussion itself shows the urgent need for
making concerted efforts to improve the accuracy of our weather and climate services. In
a country like India, where a large section of population is dependent on agriculture for its
living, correct and reliable weather prediction well in advance, will prove a boon for the
farmers. The Committee, therefore, feels that instead of putting a distant plan of achieving

17. POLAR SCIENCE AND CYROSPHERE
17.1 The Committee was informed that ‘Polar Science and Cryosphere programme’ entails the
study of the Antarctic, Arctic and Glaciers of Himalayas that are important to understand the
climate change and climate variability in the Indian region. The Arctic and Antarctic regions, and
the ocean surrounding it, are the most important areas that not only govern the earth’s climate but
are also the storehouse which archive its past climatic history. The north Atlantic and Southern
Ocean are well recognized as the major points for deep water formation that drive the large scale
thermohaline circulation in world’s oceans, thereby controlling the global climate, therefore a study
of these regions becomes important.
17.2 Explaining, the benefits of studies of Polar Regions, the Ministry explained that for a
tropical country like India, such polar processes assume greater significance as these affect the
monsoon which is the backbone of the agriculture dominated Indian economy. Recent research
have shown that natural climatic variability in polar regions such as the North Atlantic Oscillation,
Southern Hemisphere Annular Mode etc., togetherwith the Southern Ocean sea-surface-temperatures
can impart control over Indian monsoon via coupled ocean-atmosphere pathways or tele-
connections. The North Atlantic Sea Surface Temperature is strongly linked with the Indian
monsoon on inter-decadal and longer time scales. Therefore, understanding the physical
mechanisms behind these tele-connections will help India improve our predictive capability of
weather systems in northern India including the Indian monsoon. Besides, the glaciological studies
undertaken in Antarctica including monitoring of ice sheet margin, Dakshin Gangotri glacier, snow
accumulation and ablation studies, Ice core drilling and isotopic analyses of ice etc., have direct
relevance to the global warming and mass balance calculations of the ice sheet.
17.3 As regards the Budgetary allocations, the fund allocation to Arctic and Ice-Class vessel has
been provided under the programme “Polar Science and Cryosphere”, as all the activities relating
to Arctic and Antarctic including southern Ocean studies in XIIth Plan have been integrated into
this major programme. The required allocations for Arctic and and Polar Research vessel are Rs.
7.0 crores and Rs. 180.00 crores, respectively, for the year 2012-13. The Himadri station in Arctic
and Maitri and Bharati, which is in an advanced stage of commission in the Antarctic, has since
been converted in to a supply base and are the nerve centres of Indian Polar Programme from
where Indian scientists conduct front ranking research in the domains of not only atmosphere
science but also polar microbiology, upper ionosphere, solid earth geophysics, crustal evolution,
Gondwana connection of India and Antarctica etc.
17.4 The Ministry during its deliberations on the 13th April, 2012, informed the Committee that
increased number of research stations in the Polar regions would increase the base of data
collection regarding polar processes which affect the monsoon and would also facilitate climate
change studies. Moreover, as most of the glaciers in the polar regions occur at the sea level, one
can go directly to the glacier and observe them and do scientific studies, which yield meaningful
results; while at the Himalayas the Glaciers are at the height of 10,000ft and above, where studies
are difficult and any results obtained from glacial studies at polar regions could also be applied in
Himalayan regions of the country.
17.5 The Committee acknowledges the significance of the Indian polar missions as the
climatic conditions in these regions have a direct bearing on the monsoons, which is the
lifeline of the agriculture in our country. The Committee commends the setting of the
Indian polar stations which would increase the base of data collection regarding polar
processes. The Committee hopes that Bharati station would be commissioned as per

14
schedule and start its operations during the 2012-13, which will give significant boost to
India’s polar research programme. The Committee recommends that the  continuing long
term approved scientific projects which are the proposed activity under the “Polar Science
and Cryosphere”, should be pursued diligently and in a well-planned and strategic manner
and the data collected from its scientific expeditions must be analyzed and a serious
endeavor made to use the results to predict the Indian monsoons more accurately.
18. POLYMETALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME
18.1 India is a pioneer investor in the Polymetallic Nodules Programme and has 75,000sq. km.
in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB), allotted by International Sea Bed Authority of United
Nations for exploiting Polymetallic Nodules lying on the sea bed at 4000 to 6000 metre water
depth. These potato-shaped nodules contain Copper, Nickel and Cobalt which are useful elements.
The programme consists of four components - Survey and Exploration of Polymetallic Nodules in
the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB), Environmental Impact Assessment studies at CIOB,
Technology Development for mining of nodules and Technology Development for extraction of
metals from nodules.
18.2 The Comm ittee observed that the allocation for the programme ‘Polymetallic Nodules
Programme’ for the year 201 1-12, was Rs.18.00 crores at B.E. and drastically reduced to Rs.2.00
crores at R.E. stage, while for the year 2012-13, there is no allocation under this head. When the
Committee desired to know the reasons for the same, the Ministry clarified that the allocation for
‘Polymetallic Nodules Programme’ for the year 2012-13 has been provided under the programme
‘Ocean Survey and Minerals Resources’ which has been allocated Rs.68.00 crores.
18.3 The Committee was also informed of the trend of budgetary support approved and actually
utilised during the last three years. The Committee observes for the year 2009-10, there was a B.E.
allocation of Rs. 13.00 crores and the Actual expenditure was Rs.11.76 crores; while for the year
2010-11, the B.E. allocation was 15.00 crores and Actual expenditure was Rs. 12.46 crores. For
the year 2011-12 the B.E. and R.E. allocation was Rs. 18.00 crores and Rs. 2.00 crores,
respectively. The Actual expenditure for the year 2010-12 are awaited.
18.4 The Committee, notes with concern that there was a shortfall in utilisation of
allocated funds by the Ministry, to the tune of Rs. 1.24 crores in the year 2009-10 and
Rs. 2.54 crores in the year 2010-11; which is evident from the difference in B.E. and Actual
allocations for the said years. The shortfall in utilization, is even more apparent for the
year 2012, where the B.E. allocation stood reduced from Rs. 18.00 crores to Rs. 2.00 crores
only, i.e. a drastic reduction of about 90 per cent of allocated budget. The Committee takes
a serious view of the under utilisation of funds in last few years by the Ministry, which
shows that the Ministry is not seriously persuing this important programme. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry must actively pursue this
programme and the programme must be carried forward with full vigour, for exploitation of
the mineral resources in our vast Exclusive Economic Zone to enhance availability of
sufficient mineral resources required for our industrial growth.
19. GAS HYDRATES PROGRAMME
19.1 In response to a query raised by the Committee for eliciting details of initiatives taken by
the Ministry for the evaluation and quantification of gas-hydrates, in view of their potential as a
clean fuel resource, in the Indian Exclusive Economic Zone, the Ministry intimated the Committee
that under this programme, several approaches were developed for the detection, characterization,
delineation and quantification of gas-hydrates in the Krishna-Godavari (KG) and Mahanadi (Mn)
basins using the available seismic data. However, major portions of the deep-water regions have not

15
been fully explored and as most of the data which have been examined so far were acquired for
the exploration of conventional hydrocarbons, the available data were inadequate for the delineation
and assessment of gas hydrates.
19.2 The Ministry has also stated that the preliminary analysis of seismic data shows wide-spread
signatures of gas-hydrates in both the basins. By employing the indigenously developed methods for
the qualification and quantification of gas-hydrates, the Ministry is in the process of (i) ascertaining
whether the identified regions are related to gas-hydrates; (ii) understanding the petroleum system
of gas-hydrates; (iii) delineating the gas hydrate-bearing sediments; and (iv) assessing the gas-
hydrate resource potential in these regions. Ground truth verification will be carried out at the
potential locations identified through the analysis.
19.3 The Committee observes for the year 2011-12, there was a B.E. allocation of Rs.ss18.00
crores, which was reduced to Rs.11.00 crores, i.e. a reduction of Rs.7.00 crores at R.E. 2011-12.
For the year 2012-13 no separate allocation has been made under this head, however, the allocation
for ‘Gas Hydrates Programme’ for the year 2012-13 has been provided under the programme
‘Ocean Survey and Minerals Resources’ which has been allocated a total of Rs.68.00 crores.
19.4 The Committee observes that as regards the detection and quantification of gas–
hydrates, major portions of the deep-water regions have remained unexplored and available
data is inadequate for the assessment of gas-hydrates. The Committee therefore
recommends that evaluation and quantification of gas-hydrates must be intensified in the
EEZ region of the country to fully explore this resource specially in view of its potential as
clean fuel resource. The Committee is of the opinion that to meet the ever increasing
demand of energy in the country, it is imperative to explore alternate sources of energy as
soon as possible and therefore such programmes should be actively pursued and adequately
funded.
19.5 The Committee after examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants
(2012-13) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry
through its various schemes/programmes is providing a wide range of meteorological
services to people, besides carrying out high end research in meterological and polar
sciences. The Committee is therefore of the opinion that the programmes of the Ministry
of Earth Sciences should be properly and adequately funded, to provide the necessary
impetus to the core and critical programmes, Ministry has envisaged for the year 2012-13.

Commission will hardly be effective in performing its role and functions and the very
purpose of setting up of Earth Commission would be defeated. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that immediate steps be taken to provide necessary financial and
administrative powers to the Earth Commission so that it may carry out it assigned role
effectively. (Para 5.3)

been adopted by the Ministry to review and monitor physical and financial progress/
achievements of major activities with respect to agreed targets fixed for each programme,
in addition to its internal monitoring mechanisms. The Committee is of the opinion that an
effective monitoring mechanism is imperative for ensuring that the various projects are
completed as per the projected schedule and timely action taken to overcome problems that
may arise in the implementation of the projects. The Committee hopes that with potent
monitoring mechanisms, the Ministry would be able to complete its projects in time.
(Para 6.3)

to its 204th Report (page 3, para 5.1) on the Demands for Grants (2010-11), wherein it has

times during XIIth Plan with outlay proposed by the Ministry at Rs. 18,824.00 crores. The

and well before the expiry of the first year of the XIIth Plan. (Para 7.4)

crores, which is Rs. 369.00 crores less than the amount of Rs 1650.00 crores, projected by

Year Plan of the Ministry is yet to be finalised and the Ministry is not certain about some

recommends that all possible efforts may be made to finalise the XII Five Year Plan of the

of Earth Sciences and his team of officials. He informed that the Committee proposed to discuss
the functioning and Demands for Grants for the year 2012-13 of the Ministry of Earth Sciences.

Expeditions to Antarctica. Besides the Committee desired to know about the progress made in some
important programmes of the Department such as Poly metallic Nodules Programmege, Gas
Hydrates Exploration, Development of Drugs from Oceans etc. The Committee also asked the

among the Department of Space and the Ministry as regards weather forecasting. The Secretary
clarified that while the responsibility of weather forecasting lies with the Ministry, the Department
of Space, which launches the satellites, provides data, which is wholly used by the organisations
under the Ministry such as IMD, NCMRWF and INCOIS for various purposes.

the science behind earthquakes. The Ministry, in response, mentioned that it had already proposed
to set up a separate body in this regard, under the nomenclature ‘National Centre of Seismology’.

in this regard so as to recommend the setting up of such an institute to the Government.
6. During its deliberations, the Committee took up the issue of the application of Numerical
weather modeling for the purpose of weather forecast. The Ministry informed that USA is more
advanced as regards meteorological predications than India, as it not only uses a more advanced high
speed computing system than India to frame weather models but also have sufficient trained people
to run and understand those models which India, at present lacks. Therefore the Ministry proposes
To establish schools to train people in the field of meterology so that the country can attain the US
level efficiency in the next five years. While explaining the efficiency of Numerical Weather Modeling,
the Ministry stated that it represents atmospheric conditions, through a set of equations solved
through high speed computers, through which the prediction period in advance could be increased
from two to five days. He further apprised the Committee that Numerical Modeling is very important
to generate initial weather conditions based upon which future predictions are made.

Committee, the Ministry replied that Numerical Weather prediction, will bring India at par with US

25
in terms of accuracy in prediction, in the next five years and forecast improvement will take place
